bava_batra-3b-11-11.note: Rav Ashi saw cracks in the synagogue of his town, Mata Mehasya, and demolished it right away. He then brought his bed into the building site and did not take it out until the new synagogue was finished, down to the drainpipes on the roof.
bava_batra-3b-11-11.why: Rav Hisda has ruled that one may not tear down a synagogue before building its replacement, for fear it will never be rebuilt; the Gemara says this does not apply when the old building has cracks, and Rav Ashi's case shows it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who demolished his town's cracked synagogue and lived on the site until the new one was built.

bava_batra-3b-13-15.note: Herod, a slave of the Hasmonean royal house, desired one of its girls. Hearing a Divine Voice say any slave who rebels now will succeed, he killed all his masters but spared her; she cried from a roof that she was the last Hasmonean and fell to her death. Since the Sages taught that a king must be a born Jew, he killed them all, sparing only Bava ben Buta, whose eyes he put out. Hiding his identity, Herod urged Bava ben Buta to curse 'this evil slave'; he refused, citing verses and his fear. Herod revealed himself and asked how to atone. Bava ben Buta told him to rebuild the Temple, sending to Rome by a messenger slow enough that the work would be done before an answer came. Rome replied that he was a slave, not a king.
bava_batra-3b-13-15.why: The Gemara has asked how Bava ben Buta could advise Herod to tear down the Temple, when one may not demolish a synagogue before building another; it now tells the episode, and goes on to ask how he could advise a wicked ruler at all.

people.name: Herod
people.about: A slave of the Hasmonean house who killed his masters and the Sages and seized the throne.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: The one Sage Herod spared, blinded and kept as an adviser; he counsels Herod to rebuild the Temple.

terms.meaning: The Jewish royal family who ruled before Herod. The girl claims that anyone who says he descends from them is really a slave.
A voice from heaven heard announcing a message, in Aramaic and Hebrew called a 'daughter of a voice'.
The central sanctuary in Jerusalem, which Bava ben Buta calls 'the light of the world' and 'the eye of the world'.

bava_batra-5a-0-2.note: Ronya's field was surrounded on all four sides by Ravina's fields, and Ravina fenced them in. He asked Ronya to pay his share of what the fences cost, then a share at a cheap price of reeds, then just a watchman's wage; each time Ronya refused. One day, when Ronya was harvesting dates, Ravina sent his sharecropper to take a cluster, and Ronya shouted at him. Ravina said this showed Ronya valued the protection: even a goat would have to be guarded against. Ronya said one need only chase a goat away; Ravina answered that it takes a man to do the chasing. They came before Rava, who told Ronya to satisfy Ravina with what he had agreed to accept, or else be judged by the stricter ruling of Rav Huna following Rabbi Yosei.
bava_batra-5a-0-2.why: The Gemara has been debating when the owner of a field enclosed on all sides by a neighbor's fences must share their cost, as Rabbi Yosei and the first tanna disagree; Rava's ruling in this case applies that debate.

people.name: Ronya
people.about: Owner of a field enclosed by Ravina's fields, who refuses to pay toward the fences.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Neighbor who fenced in his fields all around Ronya's and asks him to share the cost.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who pushes Ronya to settle on a watchman's wage.

terms.meaning: A worker who farms another person's land in return for a share of the crop.
A Sage of the Mishna whose view, as Rav Huna rules it, would make Ronya pay half of what the fences actually cost.

bava_batra-6b-12-12.note: Two people lived in one building, one upstairs and one downstairs. The lower story began to sink until it was unfit to live in, and its owner asked the upstairs neighbor to rebuild the house with him. The upstairs neighbor said he was living comfortably. The downstairs owner offered to tear it down and rebuild it himself, and to rent the neighbor a place meanwhile; the neighbor said he did not want the bother, and told him to crawl in and out on his stomach. Rav Hama ruled that by law the upstairs neighbor may block the rebuilding. The Gemara adds that this holds only while the supporting beams are still more than ten handbreadths above the ground; once lower, the downstairs owner may say that space is his alone.
bava_batra-6b-12-12.why: The Gemara has been working out what neighbors at different heights owe each other in building and keeping up the walls between them; this case asks whether the upper resident can be forced to let the shared building be rebuilt.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Sage who ruled that the upstairs neighbor may lawfully prevent the rebuilding.

terms.meaning: A unit of length, the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters. Ten handbreadths is a common legal minimum height.

bava_batra-7a-4-5.note: A man began building a wall right outside his neighbor's windows, and the neighbor complained that it would darken his house. The builder offered to seal the windows and open new ones higher up, then to rebuild the neighbor's wall down to the windows, then down to the ground, and finally to rebuild his whole house. Each time the neighbor objected that the work would weaken his wall or that a new wall would not hold in an old house, and finally that he would have no place to live; offered a rented place, he said he did not want the bother. Rav Hama ruled that by law the neighbor may prevent the wall from being built.
bava_batra-7a-4-5.why: The Gemara asks why this case is needed, being almost the same as the upstairs neighbor who blocked a rebuilding; it answers that it teaches that one may object even if he uses the house only to store straw and wood.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Sage who ruled that the neighbor may lawfully stop the wall.

bava_batra-7b-13-15.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia made the Sages pay their share of the tax for the city wall. Reish Lakish objected that the Sages need no protection: the deeds of the righteous outnumber the sand, and if sand guards the shore against the sea, their deeds surely guard them. When Reish Lakish reported this to Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan asked why he had not quoted 'I am a wall and my breasts are like towers', and began to explain it; the explanation breaks off. In a second incident, Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda made the Sages pay the poll tax, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak told him he had broken the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings, citing a verse from each that he read as freeing Torah scholars from taxes.
bava_batra-7b-13-15.why: The Gemara has been discussing how a city's residents are made to pay for its wall and how the cost is shared; these incidents raise whether Torah scholars must pay, and Rav Yehuda then rules they are exempt from the cost of the city gates.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Leader who made the Sages pay the wall tax.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who objected that the Sages need no protection.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage to whom Reish Lakish reported, who suggests a better verse.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage who made the Sages pay the poll tax.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Sage who told him he had transgressed all three parts of the Bible.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if something holds in the weaker case, it surely holds in the stronger.
A tax charged per person, a head tax, regardless of property.

terms.term: the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings
terms.meaning: The three parts of the Hebrew Bible: the Five Books of Moses, the prophetic books, and the remaining books such as Psalms and Ezra.

bava_batra-8a-7-8.note: During years of drought, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi opened his storehouses and announced that those learned in the Bible, Mishna, Talmud, law and lore could come in for food, but the unlearned could not. Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram pushed his way in and asked to be fed. Asked whether he had studied the Bible or Mishna, he said no, and asked to be fed as a dog or a raven is fed; Rabbi fed him. Afterward Rabbi sat in distress, saying woe to him for giving his bread to an ignoramus. His son, Rabbi Shimon, suggested it might be his own disciple Yonatan ben Amram, who never wanted to benefit from the honor due to Torah. They checked and found it was so, and Rabbi said: let everyone enter.
bava_batra-8a-7-8.why: The Gemara has just ruled that Torah scholars are exempt from some city taxes because they need no protection; it adds this story of Rabbi favoring scholars, then ties it to his saying that suffering comes to the world only because of the unlearned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he opens his storehouses in a drought, at first to scholars only.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram
people.about: Rabbi's disciple, who hides his learning rather than benefit from it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son, who guesses who the visitor was.

terms.meaning: The first written collection of Jewish oral law, the core text that the Talmud discusses.
The stories, sayings and teachings of the Sages that are not law, as opposed to halakha, the law itself.
Here, a person without Torah learning.

bava_batra-8a-9-10.note: A crown tax was imposed on the city of Tiberias. Its leaders asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to make the Sages pay their share; he refused. They threatened to run away, and he told them to run. Half the city fled, and the authorities waived half the tax. The remaining half came with the same demand and threat, received the same answer, and all of them fled, leaving only one launderer. The whole tax was put on the launderer; he ran away too, and the tax was canceled. Rabbi said: you see that suffering comes to the world only because of the unlearned.
bava_batra-8a-9-10.why: Rabbi has just been shown feeding only scholars in a drought; the Gemara says this fits his view that suffering comes only because of the unlearned, and tells the incident in which he drew that lesson.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he refuses to make the Sages share the tax.

terms.meaning: A levy imposed on a city by the ruling authorities, here on Tiberias as a whole.
People without Torah learning, called 'ignoramuses' in the translation.

bava_batra-8a-16-16.note: Rabba made the orphans of the house of bar Maryon pay toward a charity. Abaye objected with a teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda that charity is not imposed on orphans, not even to redeem captives. Rabba answered that he did it to raise the orphans' standing, so that people would honor them as generous givers.
bava_batra-8a-16-16.why: The Gemara has been listing which city costs may be collected even from orphans, namely anything they benefit from; this case asks whether they may also be charged for charity.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who levied a charity contribution on the orphans of bar Maryon's household.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who challenges the levy.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: Sage whose teaching Abaye cites: no charity is imposed on orphans.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free Jews taken prisoner, one of the most pressing uses of community charity.

bava_batra-9a-1-2.note: Two butchers agreed that if either worked on the other's assigned day, his animal's hide would be torn up. One of them worked on the other's day, and the other tore up the hide. They came before Rava, who made the one who tore it pay for it. Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya objected with a teaching that townspeople may fine those who break their rules, and Rava gave no answer. Rav Pappa said Rava was right to stay silent: townspeople may make such rules only where there is no important person in the town; where there is one, they need his approval.
bava_batra-9a-1-2.why: The Gemara has cited a teaching on what a town's residents may decide for themselves, such as redirecting charity funds; Rav Yeimar's objection quotes the same teaching's power to fine, and this case sets its limit.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, here also the town's important person, who ordered the butcher to pay for the torn hide.

people.name: Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya
people.about: Sage who objected to Rava's ruling.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who explained why Rava was right not to reply.

terms.meaning: A town's leading Torah authority, whose consent the residents need before their own rules take force.

bava_batra-9b-1-4.note: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami asked Rav Sheshet how we know that a leper makes people impure during the seven days he counts toward his purification. Rav Sheshet reasoned that since the leper makes his clothes impure, he makes people impure too. Rav Ahadvoi pushed back, and each time Rav Sheshet argued from another case, Rav Ahadvoi answered that a verse states that case outright, and he said it mockingly. Rav Sheshet was deeply hurt, and Rav Ahadvoi became mute and forgot his learning. His mother, once Rav Sheshet's nursemaid, came and wept before him; he ignored her until she said: look at these breasts from which you nursed. Then he prayed for mercy for Rav Ahadvoi, and he was healed. So Rav Ahadvoi was called the infant who perverted his mother's ways.
bava_batra-9b-1-4.why: Rava has just quoted a teaching on charity from a Sage known only as the infant who perverted his mother's ways; the Gemara stops to explain the nickname, then returns to the leper question and to charity.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami
people.about: Sage who mocked Rav Sheshet and lost his speech and learning; called the infant who perverted his mother's ways.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage who was mocked; he prays for Rav Ahadvoi after his mother pleads.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi's mother
people.about: Rav Sheshet's former nursemaid, who pleads for her son.

terms.meaning: The seven days a person healed of the skin disease the Torah calls leprosy must count, partway through his purification, before bringing his offerings.
Ritually impure, a religious status that bars contact with holy things until one is purified; it is passed on by touch and other means.
One of the small creatures, such as certain rodents and lizards, whose carcass the Torah says makes a person impure.

bava_batra-10a-6-7.note: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw in a dream that his nephews were destined to lose seven hundred dinars that year. Without telling them why, he pressed them to give to charity, and took money from them for it, until only seventeen dinars of the seven hundred were left. On the eve of Yom Kippur, the government sent men who took those seventeen dinars. He told them not to fear further losses, since the seventeen were all that remained. Asked how he knew, he told them of his dream; asked why he had not told them, he said he wanted them to do the mitzva for its own sake.
bava_batra-10a-6-7.why: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shalom has just taught that a person's losses for the year are fixed at Rosh HaShana: if he merits, the money goes to charity, and if not, the government takes it. This story shows that teaching at work.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Sage who dreamt of his nephews' coming loss and steered their money into charity.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the period.
Doing a commandment, here giving charity, purely because it is right, not for what one gains by it.
The Day of Atonement, the most solemn fast day of the Jewish year, ten days after Rosh HaShana.

bava_batra-10b-4-5.note: Rabbi Abbahu says King Solomon was asked who is destined for the World-to-Come, and answered: those honored before the Elders. The Gemara illustrates with Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua, who fell ill and fainted. When he recovered, his father asked what he had seen. Yosef said he saw an upside-down world, where the important of this world were below and the lowly above; his father said he had seen a clear world. Asked how the Torah scholars fared there, Yosef said they were as important there as here. He also heard it said there: happy is one who arrives with his learning in hand, and no one can stand in the section of those executed by the government. The Gemara asks who these were, and says not Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, who would be great anyway, but martyrs like those of Lod.
bava_batra-10b-4-5.why: The Gemara is running through Rabbi Abbahu's sayings about charity and its rewards; this one turns to who earns the World-to-Come, and Yosef's vision of scholars keeping their standing there bears out Solomon's answer.

people.name: Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Fainted during an illness and on waking described the world he had seen.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Yosef's father, who asks what he saw and calls it a clear world.

people.name: Solomon
people.about: The king, asked in Rabbi Abbahu's report who is destined for the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where the righteous receive their reward.
People of the town of Lod who were killed for the sake of God's name; the Gemara says they were not Torah scholars.
Great Sages put to death by the Roman government.

bava_batra-10b-12-12.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them. She sent them to Rava, who accepted them for the sake of peace with the kingdom. When Rabbi Ami heard, he was angry, citing the verse 'When the boughs are withered, they shall be broken off', which he read to mean that a nation whose righteousness has dried up should not be helped to earn merit. The Gemara explains that Rava accepted for the sake of peace with the kingdom.
bava_batra-10b-12-12.why: The Sages have been debating a verse saying the charity of the nations is a sin for them; this incident shows two Sages differing over whether to accept charity from a gentile queen, and the Gemara goes on to reconcile them.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur of Persia, who sent money for charity.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who refused her gift and was angry that Rava accepted it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who accepted the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom.

terms.meaning: Keeping good relations with the ruling government, here by not refusing a royal gift.

bava_batra-11a-0-0.note: This is the close of the Gemara's account of a gift from the Persian queen mother to Rava, which Rabbi Ami had criticized. Rabbi Ami was angry only because the people who told him about it did not finish the report: they left out that Rava had given the money to the gentile poor, not to the Jewish poor.
bava_batra-11a-0-0.why: The Gemara has asked why Rabbi Ami objected when Rava accepted the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom; this line resolves the dispute by showing Rava had done what Rabbi Ami wanted.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: Also called Rabbi Ami; the Sage who was angry with Rava over the gift.

bava_batra-11a-1-1.note: Binyamin the righteous was in charge of the charity fund. In years of drought a woman came and begged him to feed her. He swore by the Temple service that the fund was empty. She said that if he did not feed her, a woman and her seven sons would die, so he fed her from his own money. Some time later he fell ill and was near death. The ministering angels said to God that He had taught that whoever saves one life in Israel is as if he saved a whole world; should Binyamin, who saved a woman and seven sons, die so young? At once his sentence was torn up, and a Sage taught that twenty-two years were added to his life.
bava_batra-11a-1-1.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings on the power of charity; after the debate over gifts from gentile rulers, it turns to a Jewish charity officer whose giving saved his own life, and then to King Munbaz, who gave away his treasures in a drought.

people.name: Binyamin the righteous
people.about: Supervisor of the charity fund, who fed a starving family from his own money.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, to whom the angels plead for Binyamin's life.

terms.meaning: The worship once performed in the Temple in Jerusalem; Binyamin swears an oath by it.
The angels who serve before God in heaven.

bava_batra-11a-1-3.note: Binyamin the righteous ran the community charity fund. In a year of drought a woman begged him to support her; he swore there was nothing left in the fund, and she answered that without help she and her seven sons would die. So he supported her from his own money. Later he fell deathly ill, and the ministering angels argued before God that a man who had saved a woman and seven children should not die so young. His sentence was torn up at once, and a Sage taught that twenty-two years were added to his life. A second tale follows: King Munbaz gave away his own and his ancestors' treasures in years of drought, and when his family protested, he answered with a string of verses that his ancestors stored treasure below, on earth, while he stored it above, in heaven.
bava_batra-11a-1-3.why: The Gemara has just told how Rava gave a Persian queen's gift to the gentile poor, in the middle of a discussion of charity; these two tales continue that theme by praising those who give generously in hard times, before the Gemara returns to the mishna's rules on town residents.

people.name: Binyamin the righteous
people.about: The man in charge of the charity fund, who fed a starving woman and her seven sons from his own money.

people.name: King Munbaz
people.about: A king who gave away his family's treasures to the poor during years of drought.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but is quoted in the Gemara.
The angels who serve God in heaven; here they plead with God on Binyamin's behalf.
The life after this one, in which, in rabbinic thought, a person is rewarded for good deeds.

bava_batra-12b-2-4.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi was standing in the street of Mehoza when he heard a fool announce that the next head of the yeshiva in Mata Mehasya would be a man who signs his name Tavyumei. Since he was the only Sage who signed that way, he took it as a sign his time had come and set off for Mata Mehasya. By the time he arrived, the Sages had already decided to appoint Rav Aha of Difti. When they heard he had come, they sent pairs of Sages to consult him, and he kept each pair with him until there were ten; then he began to teach and lecture, and was appointed. Rav Aha applied to himself the saying that one who is treated badly will not soon be treated well, and one who is treated well will not soon be treated badly.
bava_batra-12b-2-4.why: The Gemara is discussing whether prophecy survives among the Sages; Rabbi Yohanan says that after the Temple fell it passed to fools and children, and this incident is the Gemara's example of a fool's words coming true.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who signed his name Tavyumei and took a fool's words as a sign he would head the yeshiva.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: The Sage the others had chosen as head of the yeshiva before Mar bar Rav Ashi arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who says prophecy was given to fools and children after the Temple was destroyed.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study; its head was its chief teacher and authority.
Large public study gatherings held in the months of Elul and Adar; the text says a lecture there may not open with fewer than ten men present.

bava_batra-12b-5-5.note: Rav Hisda's young daughter was sitting on her father's lap while two Sages, Rava and Rami bar Hama, sat before him. Rav Hisda asked her which of the two she would like. She answered: both of them. Rava then said: and I will be last. The translation adds that this came true: she married Rami bar Hama first and, after he died, Rava.
bava_batra-12b-5-5.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yohanan that after the Temple was destroyed prophecy was given to fools and children; having shown a fool's words coming true, it now gives this as its example of a child's.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who jokingly asks his small daughter which of his two students she wants.

people.name: Rava
people.about: One of the two Sages sitting before Rav Hisda; he says he will be her last husband.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The other Sage sitting before Rav Hisda.

bava_batra-14a-5-5.note: Rav Huna wrote seventy Torah scrolls himself, and only once did one come out with its height exactly equal to its rolled-up circumference. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov wrote a single scroll, on calf hide, and it came out right. The Sages looked at him, and he died.
bava_batra-14a-5-5.why: The Gemara has just taught that a Torah scroll should be as tall as it is round when rolled, and that even Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not know the right size for parchment; these reports show how rarely anyone managed it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who wrote seventy Torah scrolls and got the proportions exactly right only once.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
people.about: A Sage who wrote one Torah scroll on calf hide that came out exactly right, and then died when the Sages looked at him.

terms.meaning: A handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, rolled on poles and read in the synagogue.
The translation explains this as a jealous gaze, the evil eye, which the text treats as the cause of his death.

bava_batra-16b-8-8.note: A daughter was born to Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and he was upset. His father comforted him: through daughters, increase comes into the world. Bar Kappara told Rabbi Shimon that this was empty comfort, and quoted a teaching: the world cannot exist without males and females, yet fortunate is the one whose children are sons and woe to the one whose children are daughters, just as the world needs both a spice seller and a tanner, but fortunate is the spice seller and woe to the tanner.
bava_batra-16b-8-8.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish have just disagreed whether the birth of daughters brought increase or strife into the world; this exchange plays out the same disagreement in a real family, and the Gemara next links it to a dispute over whether Abraham had a daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; upset when a daughter is born to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father, who tells him that daughters bring increase into the world.

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage who tells Rabbi Shimon that his father's comfort was empty.

terms.meaning: A worker who turns animal hides into leather, a notoriously foul-smelling trade, set against the sweet-smelling spice seller.
A teaching from the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but quoted in the Gemara.

bava_batra-22a-5-11.note: Rav Dimi of Neharde'a brought a ship of dried figs to sell. The Exilarch told Rava to see whether he was a Torah scholar, and if so to reserve the market for him. Rava sent his student Rav Adda bar Abba, who asked a hard question about an elephant that swallowed a basket and passed it whole. Rav Dimi could not answer; Rav Adda struck him on his shoe and said he was his teacher, and Rava his teacher's teacher. The market was not reserved and the figs were lost. Rav Dimi complained to Rav Yosef, who called for punishment of whoever shamed him. Rav Adda bar Abba died, and five Sages each said, I punished him. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak, kept waiting that day, said he was waiting for Rav Adda's bier, and word came that he had died; the Gemara says his words most likely caused it.
bava_batra-22a-5-11.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a town may keep outside merchants from setting up shop, but that a Torah scholar is an exception; this story shows the Exilarch applying that exception by checking whether a visiting merchant is really a scholar.

people.name: Rav Dimi of Neharde'a
people.about: A Sage who came to sell dried figs and lost them after failing Rav Adda bar Abba's test.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Abba
people.about: Rava's student, sent to test Rav Dimi; he shamed him and later died.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the Exilarch asks to check Rav Dimi; he also says he caused Rav Adda's death.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage Rav Dimi complains to; he says he cursed Rav Adda bar Abba.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Head of the kalla lectures, who reviewed his lesson daily with Rav Adda and announced he was waiting for his bier.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a leader with official standing.
To give one seller the exclusive right to sell his goods, so no one competes with him until they are sold.
An expression meaning to test someone and find out what he knows.
Large public study gatherings held in the months of Elul and Adar.

bava_batra-22b-12-12.note: Rav Yosef owned some small palm trees. Bloodletters used to sit under them to work, and crows came to eat the blood, then flew up into the trees and damaged the dates. Rav Yosef told the bloodletters to take their crows away. Abaye objected that the damage was only indirect, and that they had a long-standing right to that spot. Rav Yosef answered with rulings of other Sages: indirect damage is forbidden, and no long-standing right can be held to cause damage. When Abaye said that rule was stated only for smoke and a bathroom, Rav Yosef replied that he was sensitive, and to him this was just like smoke and a bathroom.
bava_batra-22b-12-12.why: Rav Tovi bar Mattana has just concluded from the mishna on ladders and dovecotes that causing even indirect damage is forbidden; here Rav Yosef applies that very ruling to his own trees.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage whose palm trees were damaged because of the bloodletters working beneath them.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who challenges his demand that the bloodletters leave.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that indirect damage is forbidden Rav Yosef quotes.

terms.meaning: A practitioner who drew blood from people as a medical treatment, a common remedy at the time.
Damage a person does not do himself but sets in motion, as when the bloodletters' work draws crows that ruin the dates.
A right to keep using something in a certain way because it has gone on unchallenged for a long time.

bava_batra-25b-13-13.note: Pappei Yona'a had been poor and became rich, and he built a mansion. Sesame pressers worked nearby, and when they pressed the seeds his mansion shook. He came to Rav Ashi, who told him that when they studied in Rav Kahana's study hall they used to say Rabbi Yosei concedes in the case of a person's own arrows.
bava_batra-25b-13-13.why: The mishna has Rabbi Yosei saying each neighbor may use his own land as he likes; Rav Ashi reports that even Rabbi Yosei agrees when one's activity directly strikes a neighbor, and this case shows that principle being applied.

people.name: Pappei Yona'a
people.about: A once-poor man who grew rich, built a mansion, and complained that his neighbors' sesame pressing shook it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage Pappei Yona'a came to with his complaint.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: An earlier Sage whose view Rav Ashi applies to the case.

terms.meaning: A phrase for damage that shoots out directly from a person's own activity onto a neighbor's property, like an arrow he has fired.

bava_batra-26a-8-10.note: Rava bar Rav Hanan had palm trees along the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard. Birds roosted in the palms and came down to damage the vines, so Rav Yosef told him to cut the trees down. Rava bar Rav Hanan said he had kept the required distance; Rav Yosef answered that a greater distance is needed between trees and vines. Rava bar Rav Hanan said he himself would not cut them, quoting Rav that it is forbidden to cut down a palm that yields a kav of fruit, and Rabbi Hanina that his son Shikhhat died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time. If Rav Yosef wished, he said, he could cut them himself.
bava_batra-26a-8-10.why: The mishna discusses how far trees must be planted from a neighbor's field; this case tests whether the standard distance is enough when trees stand beside a vineyard.

people.name: Rava bar Rav Hanan
people.about: Owner of palm trees on the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard, who refuses to cut them down himself.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Owner of the vineyard damaged by birds roosting in his neighbor's palms.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage quoted as saying his son Shikhhat died for cutting down a fig tree before its time.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume, a few liters; a palm yielding this much fruit is still productive.
The core law code of the early Sages, on which the Gemara comments.

bava_batra-26a-11-12.note: Rav Pappa had palm trees along the border of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua's land, and found Rav Huna digging and cutting their roots. Rav Huna cited the mishna that a man may dig three handbreadths to clear roots for his plow; when Rav Pappa said he was digging deeper, Rav Huna said he was digging cisterns, ditches and caves, where the mishna lets him cut downward. Rav Pappa said he tried every argument without success until he quoted Rav Yehuda that a strip the public has long used may not be ruined. After Rav Pappa left, Rav Huna said to himself he should have answered that this rule applies only within sixteen cubits of the tree, and he was cutting beyond that.
bava_batra-26a-11-12.why: The mishna has just ruled that a landowner may cut a neighbor's roots that spread into his field; this exchange tests how far that right goes.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of palm trees whose roots his neighbor was cutting.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Rav Pappa's neighbor, who was digging on his own land and cutting the roots.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling about land long used by the public finally persuades Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A measure of about the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.
A measure from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a meter.
The core law code of the early Sages, on which the Gemara comments.

bava_batra-29b-2-3.note: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama bought a maidservant together. One used her in the first, third and fifth years, the other in the second, fourth and sixth. Then someone came forward claiming she belonged to him. They came before Rava, who told them they had done this so that neither could establish a claim of ownership against the other; and just as their use gave them no such claim against each other, it gave them none against anyone else.
bava_batra-29b-2-3.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a presumption of ownership requires continuous use over three years; this case shows that use split into alternating years does not count.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: One of two Sages who bought a maidservant together and took turns using her year by year.

people.name: Rav Ukva bar Hama
people.about: The other partner in buying the maidservant.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who judged the case when an outsider claimed the maidservant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

bava_batra-29b-8-9.note: A man found someone living in his house and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from him and lived in it for the years needed to establish ownership. The man said he had been away in distant settlements, so he could not have protested. They came before Rav Nahman, who told the occupant to go and prove that he had lived there those years. Rava objected: is that the law? The one who seeks to take something from another must bring the proof.
bava_batra-29b-8-9.why: The Gemara is discussing what counts as a three-year presumption of ownership; this case asks who must prove the occupation when the owner says he was away, and the Gemara then notes that Rava and Rav Nahman rule the opposite way in another case.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who told the occupant to prove his years of use.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects that the burden of proof belongs on the claimant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.
The rule that whoever wants to take property from someone else must bring the evidence.

bava_batra-30b-1-2.note: A man found another working his land and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from a third person and used it for the years needed to establish ownership. The man replied that the seller was a robber who had stolen the field. The occupant said he had witnesses that he had first consulted the man, who told him to go ahead and buy. The man explained that he had said so because the occupant was easier to deal with than the robber. Rava said the claimant had stated the law correctly.
bava_batra-30b-1-2.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of disputed land; it goes on to ask whether Rava's ruling follows Admon, who accepts the same reasoning even when the claimant signed the bill of sale, and answers that a casual remark is weaker than a signature.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who accepted the original owner's explanation.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

bava_batra-30b-5-7.note: Two land disputes are told. In the first, a man found someone on his land; the occupant said he bought it from a third person and had used it the required years. The man said the seller was a robber. The occupant said he had witnesses that the man came to him at night and asked to buy it. The man said he had wanted to buy his way out of a lawsuit, and Rava said people do pay to avoid litigation. In the second, the occupant again said he bought the land and used it the required years; the claimant said he held a deed showing he had bought it from that same seller four years earlier. The occupant said by 'the required years' he meant many years, not just three, and Rava said people commonly speak that way.
bava_batra-30b-5-7.why: The Gemara is gathering Rava's rulings on contested land; these cases show which explanations of seemingly damaging behavior or words he accepted, and the Gemara then adds that the second ruling holds only if the occupant's use began before the claimant's deed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules in both disputes.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

bava_batra-31a-1-3.note: Two men disputed a piece of land, each saying it had belonged to his ancestors. One brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' land; the other brought witnesses that he had used it for the years needed to establish ownership. Rabba said the occupant should win, since he could have said he bought it from the claimant and been believed. Abaye answered that this argument does not hold when witnesses contradict him. The occupant then said: yes, it was your ancestors', but I bought it from you, and when I said it was my ancestors' I meant I relied on it as if it were.
bava_batra-31a-1-3.why: The occupant's change of story leads the Gemara to ask whether a litigant may state a claim and then revise it; Ulla says he may and the Sages of Neharde'a say he may not.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who would award the land to the occupant.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rabba because witnesses contradict the occupant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.
A legal argument: a person is believed if he could have won with a stronger claim had he wanted to lie.

bava_batra-31a-8-9.note: Two men disputed a piece of land, each saying it had belonged to his ancestors. The first brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' land and that he had used it for the years needed to establish ownership; the second brought witnesses only that he had used it for those years. Rav Nahman said the two testimonies about use cancel each other out, leaving the testimony about the ancestors, so the land goes to the first man. Rava objected that this testimony had been contradicted. Rav Nahman began to answer that although it was contradicted about the use of the land, and here the text breaks off.
bava_batra-31a-8-9.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a litigant may revise his claim; it now turns to contradictory witnesses, and next asks whether Rav Nahman and Rava differ as Rav Huna and Rav Hisda do over witnesses who contradict each other.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who awards the land to the man with witnesses about his ancestors.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects that this testimony was contradicted.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

bava_batra-31b-4-8.note: The case continues: the second man, who at first had witnesses only to his use of the land, then brought witnesses that it had belonged to his own ancestors. Rav Nahman said: we put the first man on the land and we can take him off it, and we are not worried about contempt of court. Rava, or some say Rabbi Zeira, objected from a teaching about a woman whose divorce or husband's death is disputed by two pairs of witnesses: if she remarried before contrary witnesses came, Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Yosei says she need not leave. Rav Nahman said he had meant to act, but since Rava and also Rav Hamnuna in Syria had raised this objection, he would not. Then he went out and did act. Onlookers thought he had made a mistake, but the Gemara says he relied on great authorities.
bava_batra-31b-4-8.why: The Gemara is asking whether a court that has ruled may reverse itself on new testimony; it goes on to show that this depends on a dispute among early Sages about restoring a priest's status, which is the 'great authorities' Rav Nahman relied on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who first gave the land to one man and then took it back after new witnesses came.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects to reversing the ruling; some say it was Rabbi Zeira.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who raised the same objection to Rav Nahman in Syria.

people.name: Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: An early Sage whose teaching about a remarried woman is quoted against Rav Nahman.

terms.meaning: The worry that a court which changes its rulings will look unreliable and lose respect.
A teaching from the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but quoted in the Gemara.

bava_batra-32a-6-6.note: A man found another on his land and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from him and showed a bill of sale. The man said the bill was forged. The occupant leaned over and whispered to Rabba: yes, it is forged, but I had a proper bill of sale and lost it, so I thought I would hold on to this one at least. The ruling is not given in this part of the text.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge to whom the occupant whispered his confession about the forged bill.

terms.meaning: A written document recording that land was sold, used as proof of ownership.

bava_batra-32b-2-2.note: A man demanded a hundred dinars from another and showed a promissory note. The other said the note was forged. The first man leaned over and whispered to Rava: yes, it is forged, but I had a proper note and lost it, so I thought I would hold on to this one at least. The ruling is not given in this part of the text.
bava_batra-32b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just told the same situation with a forged bill of sale for land; it brings this parallel case about money and then gives the final ruling, which treats land and money differently.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge to whom the lender whispered his confession about the forged note.

terms.meaning: A written document recording a loan, which a lender can use to collect the debt.
A coin; one hundred dinars was a sizable sum.

bava_batra-32b-8-8.note: A rumor spread that Rava bar Sharshom was living off land that belonged to orphans. Abaye asked him what had actually happened. He explained that he had held the land as collateral from the orphans' father, who also owed him other money, and had used it for the agreed years. He reasoned that if he gave it back and then claimed the other debt he would have to take an oath, so he planned to hide the collateral document and keep using the land until the debt was paid, since he could have claimed he bought it and been believed. Abaye told him he could not claim he bought it, because everyone knew it was orphans' land. He told him to return it, and to take them to court when they grew up.
bava_batra-32b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just ruled that money stays where it is when a claim rests on weak grounds; this case tests the 'he could have made a stronger claim' argument, and Abaye rejects it because the land was publicly known to be the orphans'.

people.name: Rava bar Sharshom
people.about: A Sage rumored to be living off orphans' land, which he had held as collateral from their father.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who questions Rava bar Sharshom and tells him to return the land.

terms.meaning: Property a borrower hands over to a lender as security; here the lender could use the land and its produce for a set number of years.
A solemn sworn statement in court; the Sages required one from anyone collecting a debt from orphans' property.

bava_batra-33a-3-4.note: When a relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died and left a date tree, another relative took it, each man insisting he was the closer relative. In the end the other man admitted that Rav Idi was closer, and Rav Hisda gave the tree to Rav Idi. Rav Idi then asked for the value of the dates the man had eaten since taking the tree. Rav Hisda scoffed at him: your claim rests on this man's word, and until now he said he was the closer relative, so the tree is yours only from his admission. The Gemara adds that Abaye and Rava disagree with Rav Hisda: once the man admitted, he admitted he never had a right to the fruit either.
bava_batra-33a-3-4.why: The discussion is a run of disputes over who may keep land or its produce. The next case brought also ends with Abaye and Rava rejecting a ruling of Rav Hisda, so the two cases sit side by side.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Relative of the dead man who claims the date tree and the fruit already eaten from it

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who awards the tree to Rav Idi but refuses him the past produce

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who, with Rava, disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling on the produce

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who, with Abaye, disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling on the produce

bava_batra-33b-7-7.note: A man snatched a piece of cast metal from another. The victim came before Rabbi Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting beside him, and brought a single witness to the snatching. The snatcher said: yes, I snatched it, but it was mine. Rabbi Ami was stuck: one witness is not enough to make him pay, but it is too much to let him go free, and he cannot be given an oath because by his own word he is like a robber. Rabbi Abba answered that someone who must take an oath but cannot take one has to pay.
bava_batra-33b-7-7.why: Students before Abaye thought Rabbi Abba's case settled another one: a man claiming land who brought only one witness to his years of use. Abaye then shows the two cases are not alike, since there the single witness harms the man and here he helps him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case of the snatched metal is brought

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sage sitting before Rabbi Ami who gives the ruling that settles the case

terms.meaning: In a money case, a defendant faced with only one witness against him can usually clear himself by swearing in court that the claim is false. The court does not let someone who admits to robbery swear.

bava_batra-34b-0-1.note: Two men quarreled over a boat, each saying it was his. One asked the court to hold it until he could bring witnesses; Rav Huna said the court does so, Rav Yehuda said it does not. The court took the boat, but the man found no witnesses and asked the court to let it go so that whoever was stronger would win. Rav Yehuda said the court does not release it, and Rav Pappa said it does. The Gemara rules that a court does not seize such property, but once it has seized it, it does not let it go.
bava_batra-34b-0-1.why: The discussion is about ownership disputes where neither side has proof. The next case applies the same rule, whoever is stronger prevails, and asks how it differs from cases where the property is split.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who holds the court seizes the disputed boat

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who holds the court neither seizes the boat nor, once seized, releases it

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who holds the court releases the boat once no witnesses are found

terms.meaning: A ruling used when neither side has proof or a stronger claim: the court steps aside and lets the parties settle it between themselves.

bava_batra-36a-10-10.note: In Neharde'a some goats ate a man's peeled barley. He seized the goats and claimed a large sum from their owner. Shmuel's father ruled he may claim up to the value of the goats, since he could have said the goats were his by purchase. The Gemara asks how that can be, when animals that wander do not show ownership just by being in someone's hands, and answers that goats are different because they are handed over to shepherds.
bava_batra-36a-10-10.why: The Gemara has just discussed Reish Lakish's rule that holding wandering animals does not prove ownership, and Rava's rule for slaves. This case tests that rule with livestock, and the Gemara goes on to explain why Neharde'a goats are always under guard.

people.name: Shmuel's father
people.about: The judge who rules on the claim over the goats

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage whose rule about wandering livestock the Gemara raises against the ruling

terms.meaning: The town in Babylonia where the case took place.
A standard claim: the one holding an item says he bought it. Holding it can back up that claim, so he may also make a smaller claim that is less than what that claim would give him.

bava_batra-39b-3-3.note: Giddel bar Minyumi had a protest to lodge about his land. He found Rav Huna, Hiyya bar Rav and Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi sitting together and protested before them. A year later he came back to protest again. They told him there was no need, because Rav says that once an owner has protested in the first year he need not protest again. Another version says Hiyya bar Rav told him this in his own name.
bava_batra-39b-3-3.why: The Gemara is discussing how an owner protests against someone holding his land, so the holder cannot gain ownership by three years of use. Right after this case, bar Kappara's view and Rava's ruling say a protest is needed every three years.

people.name: Giddel bar Minyumi
people.about: Landowner who lodges a protest and comes back a year later to protest again

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: One of three Sages before whom he protests

people.name: Hiyya bar Rav
people.about: One of the three Sages; in one version he gives the answer himself

people.name: Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi
people.about: One of the three Sages before whom he protests

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling the three cite: one protest in the first year is enough

terms.meaning: A formal objection by a landowner, made before witnesses, that someone is using his land wrongly. It stops the user from claiming ownership through three years of undisputed use.

bava_batra-40b-5-5.note: A man went to betroth a woman, and she said she would marry him only if he signed all his property over to her. He did. His eldest son came and asked what would become of him. The father told two witnesses to hide in a place called Avar Yemina and write a gift document for the son. When the witnesses came before Rava, he ruled that neither the son nor the wife acquired the property.
bava_batra-40b-5-5.why: Rav Yehuda has said a concealed gift document cannot be collected, and Rava was reported to hold that it cancels a later gift. Rav Pappa tells this case to show that report was only an inference; the Gemara then explains the wife lost because the gift to her was made under pressure.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who rules that neither the son nor the wife acquired the property

terms.meaning: A gift document written in secret at the giver's request. Because it is hidden, the Sages suspect it was not meant seriously, and it cannot be used to collect.

bava_batra-41a-6-8.note: A flood swept through Rav Anan's land and knocked down the boundary wall between his land and his neighbor's. Rav Anan rebuilt it but put it on his neighbor's land. Rav Nahman told him to move it back. Rav Anan objected that he had already taken possession, and Rav Nahman answered that the rule that possession in the owner's presence counts at once is not the law. Rav Anan said the neighbor had given up the land by helping him build the wall, and Rav Nahman replied that the neighbor did not know, just as Rav Anan did not.
bava_batra-41a-6-8.why: The mishna has just taught that holding land proves nothing without a claim to it. This is the first of a series of cases, marked by a short memory aid, about when taking hold of land gives a right to it.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Landowner who rebuilds his washed-out wall on his neighbor's land

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the wall moved back

terms.meaning: A right to land gained by using it openly, normally for three years, without the former owner protesting.

bava_batra-41a-9-9.note: A flood swept through Rav Kahana's field and knocked down his boundary wall, and he rebuilt it on land that was not his. His neighbor brought two witnesses: one said the wall had gone two rows into the neighbor's land, the other said three. Rav Yehuda told Rav Kahana to pay two of the three rows. Rav Kahana asked if he was following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that witnesses who differ like this still combine for the smaller amount, and said he could bring a letter from the Land of Israel showing the law is not so. Rav Yehuda answered: when you bring it.
bava_batra-41a-9-9.why: It follows Rav Anan's matching case of a wall rebuilt on a neighbor's land. Here the question shifts to two witnesses who do not agree on how much land was taken.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Landowner who rebuilds his washed-out wall on land that is not his

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The judge who orders Rav Kahana to pay two rows

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sage whose account of a dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel Rav Kahana cites

terms.meaning: The schools of the early Sages Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on points of law.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
The Babylonian Sages' name for the Land of Israel.

bava_batra-41b-4-5.note: A man had lived in a loft in Kashta for four years when the former owner came and asked what he was doing in his house. The man said he had bought it from someone who had bought it from the owner. Rabbi Hiyya told him that if he had witnesses that the seller had lived there, even for one day, the house would stay his; if not, it would not. Rav, his nephew, recalls asking him whether people do not often buy a house and sell it the same night, and he saw that Rabbi Hiyya would believe the man if he said the seller had bought it from the owner in his presence.
bava_batra-41b-4-5.why: The discussion is about claims that come with holding land. Right after this, Rava tries to support Rabbi Hiyya's ruling from the mishna about inherited land, and the Gemara rejects the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The judge in the case of the loft; Rav calls him his uncle

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, who sat before him and questioned his ruling

bava_batra-46a-7-8.note: Abaye told Rava to come and see what the swindlers of Pumbedita do. A man asks a craftsman for his cloak back, and the craftsman says it never happened. The man says he has witnesses who saw it with him; the craftsman says that was a different cloak, and when asked to bring it out, he refuses. Rava answered that the craftsman's claim holds, since the owner must have seen his own cloak there. Rav Ashi said a clever owner can get him to bring it out by asking it to be valued against any debt, and Rav Aha son of Rav Avya replied that a clever craftsman can say it was already valued.
bava_batra-46a-7-8.why: The Gemara has been teaching laws about items left with a craftsman, including a teaching that an owner has a claim only if he saw his item there. Rava uses that teaching to back the craftsman.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who points out the trick of the Pumbedita craftsmen

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who holds that the craftsman's claim is accepted

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who suggests how a clever owner can get the cloak brought out

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya
people.about: Sage who answers Rav Ashi with the craftsman's counter-move

terms.meaning: A town in Babylonia known for its Torah academy.

bava_batra-48b-6-6.note: A man named Tavi hung another man, Pafi, on a kinara and forced him to sell his field. Rabba bar bar Hana signed both Pafi's declaration that the sale was forced and the bill of sale. Rav Huna said that whoever signed the declaration did well, and whoever signed the bill of sale also did well.
bava_batra-48b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a sale made under force is valid. It then asks how Rav Huna can approve both documents, and explains him by his own rule that a forced sale stands.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Man who hangs Pafi and forces him to sell his field

people.name: Pafi
people.about: Man forced to sell his field

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Sage who signs both the declaration and the bill of sale

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who says both signings were right

terms.meaning: Usually understood as a kind of tree or thorn bush; Pafi was hung on one to force him to sell.
A statement made before witnesses ahead of a sale or gift, saying it is being done under force and is not truly wanted. It can cancel the transaction.
The document that records a sale of land.

bava_batra-52a-2-2.note: When the wife of Rabba bar bar Hana was dying, she said that rings she had belonged to Marta and to the sons of her daughter. Rabba bar bar Hana came before Rav to ask what to do. Rav told him: if she is credible in your eyes, do as she said; if not, ignore her words. Another version says Rav told him to judge how likely it was that the rings had been left with her.
bava_batra-52a-2-2.why: A teaching the Gemara has just quoted says that when a woman, slave or child declares at death that an item belongs to someone, the bailee follows them if believable and ignores them if not. Rav applies that rule to this case.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Husband who asks what to do with the rings after his wife's dying words

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who tells him how to treat her words

people.name: Marta
people.about: Person his wife named as owner of the rings

bava_batra-54a-5-5.note: A woman had cut branches from an ownerless palm tree for thirteen years. Then another man came and plowed a little beneath it. The case came before Levi, or by another account Mar Ukva, who gave the tree to the man who plowed. The woman came and shouted before him, and he said to her: what can I do for you, since you did not take possession the way people take possession?
bava_batra-54a-5-5.why: Shmuel has been listing acts that do or do not acquire ownerless land, depending on whether they improve the field. This case shows that years of cutting branches did not count, while a little plowing did.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Sage before whom the case came in one version

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Sage before whom the case came in another version, who answers the woman

terms.meaning: Land or goods that belong to no one, such as the estate of a convert who died without heirs. The first person to perform a proper act of possession acquires it.

bava_batra-54b-4-4.note: Rav Huna bought land from a non-Jew, and another Jew came and plowed it a little. They came before Rav Nahman, who gave the land to the man who plowed. Rav Huna asked whether he was relying on Shmuel's rule that a non-Jew's property is like a desert, open to the first who takes it. If so, he said, let him also follow Shmuel's other rule, that one who hoes acquires only the spot he hoed. Rav Nahman answered that on this point he follows the teaching that one stroke of the hoe acquires the whole field.
bava_batra-54b-4-4.why: The Gemara has quoted Shmuel's rule about land bought from a non-Jew, and Abaye has questioned it because land law requires a deed. This case shows the rule being applied, and a ruling follows that the land is not taken from the second Jew.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Buyer of land from a non-Jew, which another Jew then plowed

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who gives the land to the man who plowed

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose two rulings Rav Huna quotes

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling that one stroke of a hoe acquires the whole field Rav Nahman follows

terms.meaning: Ownerless. Shmuel's term for land a non-Jew has sold for money but whose buyer has not yet received the deed.

bava_batra-58a-2-5.note: Rabbi Bena'a was marking burial caves. At the cave of Abraham he found Eliezer, Abraham's servant, standing at the entrance, who told him Abraham was lying in Sarah's arms while she examined his head. Rabbi Bena'a asked to be announced; Eliezer told him to enter, since in that world there is no evil inclination, and he went in, examined the cave and left. At Adam's cave a Divine Voice told him he had looked at the likeness of God's image but must not look at the image itself, and that the inner cave measures the same as the outer. Rabbi Bena'a says he saw Adam's heels, and they were like two suns.
bava_batra-58a-2-5.why: The Gemara has been quoting teachings about how Torah scholars keep their tables and beds. It says it tells this story because Rabbi Bena'a was just mentioned.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage marking burial caves who enters the cave of Abraham

people.name: Eliezer
people.about: Abraham's servant, standing at the cave entrance

people.name: Abraham
people.about: Lies in the cave in Sarah's arms

people.name: Sarah
people.about: Abraham's wife, examining his head

people.name: Adam
people.about: The first man, whose cave Rabbi Bena'a is told not to look into; he saw his heels

terms.meaning: Graves were marked so that priests and others could avoid becoming ritually impure by contact with the dead.
A voice from heaven that speaks in Talmud stories.
The urge in a person toward sin, here including sexual desire.

bava_batra-58a-7-7.note: A magus was rummaging through graves. When he reached the burial cave of Rav Tovi bar Mattana, Rav Tovi grabbed him by the beard and would not let go. Abaye came and begged him to release the man. A year later the magus came again, and Rav Tovi grabbed his beard again. This time he would not let go even when Abaye asked, until Abaye brought scissors and cut off the beard.
bava_batra-58a-7-7.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Bena'a marking burial caves, as another tale about burial caves.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: Dead Sage in whose burial cave the magus is caught

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who asks Rav Tovi to release the magus, and in the end cuts off the beard

terms.meaning: A Persian priest. The Gemara often mentions them disturbing graves.

bava_batra-58a-8-8.note: A dying man told his family: a barrel of earth to one son, a barrel of bones to another, and a barrel of wads of wool to a third. No one knew what he meant, so they came to Rabbi Bena'a. He asked whether their father had left land, livestock and quilts, and they said yes. Then that was his meaning, he told them: land to one son, livestock to the second and quilts to the third.
bava_batra-58a-8-8.why: It is the first of a set of Rabbi Bena'a stories, told after the account of him marking burial caves.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage who works out the dying man's riddle

bava_batra-58a-8-10.note: A man overheard his wife tell their daughter to keep her affairs hidden, since she herself had ten sons and only one was by the girl's father. When he was dying he said: all my property to one son. The family did not know which, and came to Rabbi Bena'a. He told the sons to go strike their father's grave until he rose and told them; they all went except one, and Rabbi Bena'a gave everything to the one who stayed away. The other brothers, angry, slandered him at the king's court as a man who takes people's money without witnesses, and he was arrested and imprisoned. The text here does not say how it ended.
bava_batra-58a-8-10.why: It is one of a series of stories about Rabbi Bena'a's wisdom, told after the account of him marking burial caves.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage who finds out which son is the dying man's true son, and is imprisoned for it

bava_batra-58a-11-13.note: While Rabbi Bena'a was in prison, his wife told the guards a riddle: she had one servant whose head they cut off, whom they skinned and ate, filled with water and gave friends to drink from, without paying her. No one understood, so they called the wise man of the Jews, Rabbi Bena'a, who explained that she meant a goat made into a water skin. Impressed, they had him sit as a judge at the gate. He corrected two inscriptions there: a judge summoned to court is unfit only if money is lawfully taken from him, and blood is first of all illness, wine first of all healing. Each time they added: the elders of the Jews say so.
bava_batra-58a-11-13.why: It continues the Rabbi Bena'a stories: after his ruling about the dead man's sons, his brothers had him put in prison, and this is how he got out.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Imprisoned Sage who explains his wife's riddle and becomes a judge at the gate

people.name: The wife of Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Tells the guards a riddle while her husband is in prison

terms.meaning: The city gate, where judges sat to hear cases.

bava_batra-60a-10-11.note: Rabbi Ami had a projection from his house sticking out into an alleyway. Another man had one sticking out into the public street, and the public objected. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told him to cut it off. The man said: but you have one too. Rabbi Ami answered that his own stuck out into an alleyway, whose few residents had agreed to it, while the man's stuck out into the public street, and no one can agree on behalf of the public.
bava_batra-60a-10-11.why: The mishna has just taught that one may not build projections or balconies out over the public domain. Rabbi Ami's case applies that rule and is followed by a similar story about Rabbi Yannai and a tree.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage with a projection into an alleyway who orders the man to cut his own

terms.meaning: A beam or part of a building that sticks out from the wall over the street or alley.
Streets and places that belong to everyone, not to particular residents.

bava_batra-60a-12-12.note: Rabbi Yannai owned a tree that leaned out over the public road, and so did another man. The public objected to the other man's tree, and he came to Rabbi Yannai for a ruling. Rabbi Yannai told him to go and come back tomorrow, and that night he had his own tree cut down. When the man returned, Rabbi Yannai told him to cut his tree. The man protested that the master had one too, and Rabbi Yannai answered: go and look; if mine is cut down, cut yours, and if not, you need not cut yours either.
bava_batra-60a-12-12.why: The mishna forbids things that jut out into the public domain, and Rabbi Ami has just ordered a man to cut a projection. The Gemara then explains Rabbi Yannai's delay with Reish Lakish's teaching: set yourself right first, and only then correct others.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage whose own tree leaned over the public road; the man brings his case to him.

people.name: a certain man
people.about: Owner of another leaning tree, whom the public wanted to make cut it down.

terms.meaning: Streets and roads that belong to everyone; an owner may not let his property block or overhang them.

bava_batra-60b-10-12.note: After the Second Temple was destroyed, many Jews became ascetics who refused to eat meat or drink wine, because meat had been offered on the altar and wine poured on it, and the altar was gone. Rabbi Yehoshua joined them and argued: then we should not eat bread, since the meal-offerings have ceased; they answered they could live on produce. Then not fruit, since the first fruits have ceased; they said other produce would do. Then not water, since the water libation has ceased. They fell silent. He told them that not mourning at all is impossible, but mourning too much is also impossible, since the Sages impose no decree that most of the public cannot keep.
bava_batra-60b-10-12.why: The Gemara has been discussing a ruling that people may not plaster their houses as a sign of mourning for the Temple. Rabbi Yehoshua's answer to the ascetics leads into the measured rule that follows: plaster the house, but leave a small patch bare in remembrance.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who reasons with the ascetics and teaches them how to mourn.

terms.meaning: People who deny themselves ordinary pleasures; here, Jews who gave up meat and wine in mourning.
Offerings of flour brought on the Temple altar.
The first produce of the harvest, which farmers once brought to the Temple.
A ceremony in the Temple in which water was poured on the altar.

bava_batra-73a-7-7.note: Rabba reports what seafarers told him: when a wave that is about to sink a ship comes with a ray of white fire at its head, they strike it with clubs inscribed with names of God, and the wave calms down.
bava_batra-73a-7-7.why: The Gemara has been discussing what is included when a ship is sold, and from there turns to a series of tales about ships and the sea.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who passes on what sailors told him.

bava_batra-73a-8-9.note: Rabba passes on a seafarers' tale. Waves can be three hundred parasangs apart and three hundred parasangs high. Once a wave lifted their ship so high that they saw the resting place of a small star, as large as a field sown with forty se'a of mustard seed, and had it lifted them higher they would have been scorched. Then one wave called to another: did you leave anything in the world unwashed, that I may destroy it? The other answered: see the power of your Master; I cannot pass even a strip of sand, and it quoted Jeremiah's verse about God setting sand as the bound of the sea.
bava_batra-73a-8-9.why: It follows the Gemara's discussion of what comes with a ship that is sold, as part of a run of tales about ships and the sea.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who passes on what sailors told him.

terms.meaning: An ancient Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
A measure of volume for grain or seed; forty se'a of mustard seed would sow a large field.

bava_batra-73a-10-10.note: Rabba says he saw Hurmin, son of Lilith, running along the tops of the walls of Mehoza so fast that a horseman riding below could not catch him. Once two mules were saddled for him, standing on two bridges of the river Rognag, and he leapt from one to the other and back, pouring wine between two cups in his hands without spilling a drop, on a stormy day. Word of this reached the king's house, and they killed him.
bava_batra-73a-10-10.why: It is one of a series of marvels the Gemara collects after the seafarers' tales.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who says he saw these things himself.

people.name: Hurmin, son of Lilith
people.about: A demon-like figure who performs impossible feats until the king's men kill him.

terms.meaning: In Jewish lore, a female demon; calling Hurmin her son marks him as a supernatural being.

bava_batra-73b-1-1.note: Rabba says he saw a day-old antelope as big as Mount Tabor, which is four parasangs. Its neck was three parasangs long and the place where its head rested was a parasang and a half. Its dung dammed up the Jordan River.
bava_batra-73b-1-1.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who says he saw this himself.

terms.meaning: An ancient Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.

bava_batra-73b-2-2.note: Rabba bar bar Hana says he saw a frog as big as the fort of Hagronya, which is the size of sixty houses. A snake came and swallowed the frog, then a raven came and swallowed the snake and flew up to sit in a tree. Think how strong that tree must have been. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel said that had he not been there, he would not have believed it.
bava_batra-73b-2-2.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who says he was there, and would not have believed it otherwise.

bava_batra-73b-3-3.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a huge fish that had been killed by a tiny mud-eating creature lodged in its nostril. The sea threw it on the shore, and it destroyed sixty districts; sixty districts ate from it and sixty salted its meat, and three hundred flasks of oil were filled from one eyeball. When they came back a year later, people were sawing beams from its bones to rebuild the districts it had destroyed.
bava_batra-73b-3-3.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

bava_batra-73b-4-4.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a fish so old that sand had settled on its back and grass grew there. Thinking it was dry land, they climbed onto it and baked and cooked. When its back grew hot, the fish turned over, and had the ship not been close by they would have drowned.
bava_batra-73b-4-4.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

bava_batra-73b-5-5.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which the ship sailed for three days and three nights between one fin of a fish and the other, the fish swimming upstream and the ship downstream. Lest anyone think the ship was slow, Rav Dimi said such a ship covers sixty parasangs in the time it takes to heat a kettle of water, and outran an arrow shot by a horseman. Rav Ashi said the fish was a sea gildana, which has two sets of fins.
bava_batra-73b-5-5.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who adds how fast such a ship travels.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who names the kind of fish.

terms.meaning: An ancient Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.

bava_batra-73b-6-6.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of a voyage on which they saw a bird standing in water up to its ankles, with its head in the sky. Thinking the water was shallow, they wanted to go down to cool off, but a Divine Voice told them not to: a carpenter's ax had fallen in there seven years earlier and still had not reached the bottom, because the water is so turbulent. Rav Ashi said the bird was the ziz sadai named in Psalms.
bava_batra-73b-6-6.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who identifies the bird from a verse in Psalms.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven that, in Talmudic stories, speaks to people to announce or warn.
A creature named in Psalms 50:11, understood here as a giant bird.

bava_batra-73b-7-7.note: Rabba bar bar Hana tells of crossing the desert and seeing geese so fat their wings drooped, with streams of oil flowing beneath them. He asked them: will we have a share of you in the World-to-Come? One raised a wing and one raised a leg. When he told Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Elazar said the Jewish people will be held to account for those geese.
bava_batra-73b-7-7.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage to whom Rabba bar bar Hana reports what he saw.

terms.meaning: The life and reward the righteous receive after this world.

bava_batra-73b-9-10.note: Crossing the desert, Rabba bar bar Hana traveled with an Arab who could tell the road, and how far they were from water, by smelling the dust; Rabba bar bar Hana tried to trick him by switching the dust and could not. The Arab showed him the dead of the wilderness, the Israelites who died after leaving Egypt, lying on their backs and looking drunk, so huge that the Arab rode a camel under one man's raised knee with his spear upright.
