Rabba bar bar Hana cut a corner of one of their fringed garments, and they could not move until he returned it. When he told the Sages, they called him a donkey and an idiot: if he wanted to settle how many threads belong in fringes, he should simply have counted them.
bava_batra-73b-9-10.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by Rabba and Rabba bar bar Hana, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: A desert guide who reads the land by smelling dust and leads Rabba bar bar Hana to the dead of the wilderness.

people.name: the Sages
people.about: The scholars who rebuke Rabba bar bar Hana when he reports what he did.

terms.meaning: Threads tied to the corners of a garment, as the Torah commands; some were dyed sky-blue.
Two early schools of Sages who often disagreed; here, over how many threads go into the fringes.

bava_batra-74a-2-3.note: The Arab guide also took Rabba bar bar Hana to Mount Sinai, which was ringed by scorpions as tall as white donkeys. There he heard a Divine Voice saying: woe is Me that I took an oath, and now who will release Me from it? When he told the Sages, they called him a donkey and an idiot, saying he should have answered: your oath is released. The Gemara explains that he thought it might be God's oath never to bring another flood, and the Sages reply that then God would not have said woe is Me.
bava_batra-74a-2-3.why: It is one of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, part of a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: the Arab
people.about: The desert guide who leads Rabba bar bar Hana to Mount Sinai.

people.name: the Sages
people.about: The scholars who rebuke Rabba bar bar Hana.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven that, in Talmudic stories, speaks to people to announce or warn.
A Sage may declare a person's vow or oath void; the Sages say Rabba bar bar Hana should have done so for God.

bava_batra-74a-4-4.note: The Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana the place where Korah's followers were swallowed by the earth: two cracks giving off smoke. The Arab dipped a tuft of wool in water, put it on the tip of his spear and held it in, and it came out scorched. He told Rabba bar bar Hana to listen, and he heard them saying: Moses and his Torah are true, and we are liars. The Arab said that every thirty days Gehenna brings them back to this spot, like meat turning in a pot, and each time they say this.
bava_batra-74a-4-4.why: It is one of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, part of a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: the Arab
people.about: The desert guide who shows him the place and tests it with wool on a spear.

people.name: Korah
people.about: Leader of a rebellion against Moses; his followers here cry out from the earth that swallowed them.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment for the wicked after death.

bava_batra-74a-5-5.note: The Arab guide offered to show Rabba bar bar Hana the place where earth and sky touch. Rabba bar bar Hana set his basket down in a window of the sky, and when he finished praying it was gone. He asked whether there were thieves here. The Arab said no: the sphere of the heavens was turning, and if he waited until tomorrow he would find it again.
bava_batra-74a-5-5.why: It is the last of the sights an Arab guide showed Rabba bar bar Hana in the desert, in a long run of travelers' marvels the Gemara strings together.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The narrator, telling what he says he saw on his travels.

people.name: the Arab
people.about: The desert guide who explains where the basket went.

terms.meaning: The ancient picture of the sky as a great dome that turns around the earth.

bava_batra-74a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yohanan tells of a voyage on which they saw a crate set with precious stones and pearls, circled by sharks. A diver went down to bring it up, and the sharks, enraged, tried to tear off his thigh, but he threw a flask of vinegar at them and they sank away. Then a Divine Voice told them: what business do you have with the crate of the wife of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa? She is destined to put sky-blue wool in it for the fringes of the righteous in the World-to-Come.
bava_batra-74a-7-7.why: It is one of a run of sea tales the Gemara strings together, this one told by Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who tells what he saw on a voyage.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose wife, the Divine Voice says, owns the crate.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven that, in Talmudic stories, speaks to people to announce or warn.
Wool dyed a special blue, used for one thread of the ritual fringes on a garment's corners.
The life and reward the righteous receive after this world.

bava_batra-74b-1-1.note: Rav Yehuda from India tells of a voyage on which they saw a precious stone circled by a sea serpent. A diver went down for it, and the serpent tried to swallow the ship. A raven cut off its head and the water turned to blood. Another serpent came, hung the stone on the dead one, and it came back to life and again tried to swallow the ship. A bird cut off its head and threw the stone onto the ship. The travelers had some salted birds with them; they put the stone on them, and the birds took the stone and flew away with it.
bava_batra-74b-1-1.why: It closes a run of travelers' tales about sea creatures; the Gemara then turns to the great sea creatures mentioned in the Bible.

people.name: Rav Yehuda from India
people.about: The Sage who tells what he saw on a voyage.

bava_batra-74b-2-2.note: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were traveling by ship. Rabbi Eliezer was asleep and Rabbi Yehoshua awake, and Rabbi Yehoshua trembled, waking Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Eliezer asked why he trembled, and Rabbi Yehoshua said he had seen a great light in the sea. Rabbi Eliezer answered that perhaps he had seen the eyes of the leviathan, quoting Job: his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.
bava_batra-74b-2-2.why: After the travelers' tales of huge sea creatures, the Gemara turns to the sea creatures of the Bible; this account opens its discussion of the leviathan and the great sea monsters of Genesis.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage traveling by ship who suggests what his companion saw.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who sees a great light in the sea and trembles.

terms.meaning: A giant sea creature described in the Bible, especially in the book of Job.

bava_batra-74b-3-3.note: Rav Ashi reports that Huna bar Natan told him: crossing the desert with a thigh of meat, they cut it open, removed the forbidden sinew and fat, and laid it on the grass. By the time they brought firewood the meat had healed itself whole, and they roasted it. A year later they came back and found the coals still glowing. Ameimar explained that the grass was a herb of life and the coals were from broom wood.
bava_batra-74b-3-3.why: It is one of a long run of travelers' marvels, told by various Sages, that the Gemara strings together one after another.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who passes on what Huna bar Natan told him.

people.name: Huna bar Natan
people.about: The traveler who tells what happened to the meat.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who explains the grass and the coals.

terms.meaning: Parts of an animal that Jewish law forbids eating: the sciatic nerve of the thigh and certain fats.
A desert shrub whose wood was known for burning a very long time.

bava_batra-75a-9-10.note: Rabbi Yohanan taught that in the future God will set huge precious stones and pearls, thirty by thirty cubits with openings ten by twenty, in the gates of Jerusalem. A student sneered: we cannot even find a gem the size of a dove's egg. Later, at sea, the student saw ministering angels sawing exactly such stones and was told they were for Jerusalem's gates. He came back and told Rabbi Yohanan he had seen it just as he said. Rabbi Yohanan called him worthless, said he had believed only because he had seen and was mocking the words of the Sages, and set his eyes on him; the student was killed and turned into a pile of bones.
bava_batra-75a-9-10.why: The Gemara is interpreting Isaiah's verses about the future glory of Jerusalem, and brings this story to explain the words "your gates of precious stones." Afterward it questions how gates ten by twenty cubits fit with teachings that people will then be a hundred cubits tall.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage teaching about the future gates of Jerusalem.

people.name: A certain student
people.about: An unnamed student who mocked Rabbi Yohanan's teaching and later saw it confirmed.

terms.meaning: Angels who serve God; here the student finds them preparing the gems for Jerusalem.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a meter.

bava_batra-77b-2-2.note: Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars held for him by others in Bei Hozai. He transferred ownership of that money to his agent, Rav Shmuel bar Aha, by means of the threshold of his house, so that the agent could go and collect it. When Rav Shmuel bar Aha came back with the money, Rav Pappa was so glad that he went out as far as Tavakh to greet him.
bava_batra-77b-2-2.why: The Gemara has just said that money, which cannot be acquired by a symbolic exchange, can be transferred along with land. Rav Pappa's handing over distant money "by means of" his threshold is brought as an example of that.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of money held for him in Bei Hozai.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Aha
people.about: Rav Pappa's agent, who received the money and brought it back.

terms.meaning: A legal method in which movable goods or money pass to the new owner together with a piece of land he acquires, even if the goods are far away.
A silver coin; twelve thousand dinars was a large sum.

bava_batra-82b-14-15.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that in Tzalmon a man planted his vineyard with sixteen cubits between rows. Each year he bent the branches of two facing rows to one side and sowed grain in the cleared strip, then switched sides the next year. The case came before the Sages and they permitted it. Separately, Rav Yosef recalls a case of trees sold in a village of shepherds that came before Rav Yehuda, who told the seller to give the buyer land "sufficient for an ox and its vessels"; Rav Yosef did not know how much that was until he heard a mishna about keeping trees four cubits from a neighbor's field.
bava_batra-82b-14-15.why: The Gemara is asking how far apart three trees may be and still count as one unit. Abaye points to the Tzalmon ruling to support a sixteen-cubit limit, and Rav Yosef answers with Rav Yehuda's ruling, which he takes to mean four cubits.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the Tzalmon vineyard case.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Answers Abaye by recalling a case he saw decided.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The judge who ruled in the shepherds' village case.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the Tzalmon case asks whether sowing between widely spaced rows breaks it.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings that the Gemara discusses and cites.

bava_batra-88a-5-7.note: A man walked into a butcher shop and lifted a thigh of meat to look at it; while he held it, a horseman came and seized it from him. He came before Rav Yeimar, who made him pay the butcher its value. In another case, a man brought pumpkins to Pum Nahara and everyone took one without paying yet; angry, he declared the pumpkins consecrated to Heaven. They came before Rav Kahana, who said a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.
bava_batra-88a-5-7.why: Shmuel has just ruled that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to examine it is liable if it breaks, when its price is fixed. Both cases apply that idea: where the price is fixed, lifting the item works like completing the purchase.

people.name: Rav Yeimar
people.about: Judge who made the buyer pay for the meat seized from his hands.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Judge who ruled that the pumpkin seller's consecration had no effect.

terms.meaning: Declared the property of the Temple, so that no one else may use it.
Where an item's price is set and known, so that picking it up shows the buyer has agreed to the deal.

bava_batra-89a-8-9.note: The house of the Nasi appointed market inspectors to supervise both measures and prices. Shmuel told his student Karna to go out and teach them that inspectors are appointed for measures but not for prices. Karna went out and taught instead that they are appointed for both. Shmuel asked his name, and when he answered "Karna," Shmuel said: let a horn grow in his eye. A growth came out in Karna's eye.
bava_batra-89a-8-9.why: The Gemara is drawing rules from the Torah's demand for honest weights and measures, and a teaching that courts appoint inspectors for measures but not prices; the story shows Shmuel holding to that, while the Gemara says Karna followed Rabbi Yitzhak, who allows inspectors for prices too.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The teacher who sent Karna to correct the Nasi's household.

people.name: Karna
people.about: Shmuel's student, who taught the opposite of his instructions.

terms.meaning: The Patriarch, the official head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; his household made appointments like these.
Officials who checked that merchants used accurate measures, and, in some views, fair prices.
The student's name, which also means "horn" in Aramaic; Shmuel's curse plays on it.

bava_batra-100b-6-6.note: The sister of Rami bar Pappa was married to Rav Avya. When she died, Rav Avya performed the ceremony of standing and sitting for her. Rav Yosef said he made two mistakes: the ceremony is done only with close relatives and he did it even with distant ones, and it is done only on the first day and he did it on the second day.
bava_batra-100b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just described the mourners' practice of stopping seven times on the way back from a burial. Rav Avya's case is used to set its limits, and Abaye and Rava go on to add further errors he made.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: Husband of Rami bar Pappa's sister; held the ceremony when she died.

people.name: Rami bar Pappa
people.about: Brother of Rav Avya's wife.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who said Rav Avya erred in two ways.

terms.meaning: A mourning rite in which those returning from a burial stop and sit, then stand and walk on, several times, to honor the dead.

bava_batra-106a-5-5.note: Rav Pappa bought land from a man who told him it was a field of twenty griv. When Rav Pappa measured it, it held only fifteen. He came before Abaye, who told him: you knew what you were buying and accepted it. Rav Pappa objected that the mishna lets a buyer deduct for a shortfall; Abaye answered that this holds only for a buyer unfamiliar with the field. Rav Pappa objected that the seller had said twenty; Abaye answered that he meant the field was as good as one of twenty.
bava_batra-106a-5-5.why: The mishna has been ruling on fields sold by stated size that turn out smaller, and the Gemara is debating exactly how much of a shortfall is allowed. Rav Pappa's case adds that a buyer who already knew the field cannot claim the difference.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Bought a field that turned out smaller than the seller said.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Judge who ruled against Rav Pappa.

terms.meaning: A measure of land by how much seed it takes to sow; twenty griv here means a field fit for twenty se'a of grain.
The early collection of rabbinic teachings; here its rule on fields sold with a stated size.

bava_batra-111a-10-11.note: Rabbi Yannai, whose eyes were dim, walked leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, when Rabbi Yehuda Nesia came toward them. Rabbi Simlai said the man coming was handsome and so was his cloak. When he reached them, Rabbi Yannai felt the cloak and said it was as coarse as sackcloth. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asked how we know a son comes before a daughter in inheriting a mother's property; Rabbi Yannai derived it from a verse linking the mother's tribe to the father's. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objected that then a firstborn should take a double portion of a mother's property too. Rabbi Yannai told his attendant: take me away, this man does not want to learn.
bava_batra-111a-10-11.why: The Gemara has been rejecting the view that a son and daughter inherit equally from their mother. This story gives the source for a son coming first, and Abaye then answers the question Rabbi Yannai brushed aside.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: An elderly Sage with dim eyes, led by his attendant.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: Rabbi Yannai's attendant, on whose shoulder he leaned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The man who approached them and asked about inheritance.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who later explains why a firstborn gets no double share of a mother's property.

terms.meaning: The Torah gives a firstborn son twice the share of each other son in his father's estate.
A method of reading in which two things mentioned together in a verse are taken to share the same rules.

bava_batra-115b-1-5.note: The Sadducees held that a daughter inherits together with a son's daughter. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai confronted them: fools, where do you get this? No one could answer except an old man who chattered that if a son's daughter inherits, the man's own daughter surely should. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai cited verses about Zibeon and Anah to show grandchildren count as children. The Sadducee said, Master, you dismiss me with this? Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai called him a fool and broke his argument: a son's daughter is stronger because she inherits beside her father's brothers, while a daughter is weaker, since she does not inherit beside her brothers. The Sages won, and made that day, the twenty-fourth of Tevet, a festival.
bava_batra-115b-1-5.why: The Gemara has been setting the order of heirs, with a son's descendants ahead of a daughter. Rav Huna, quoting Rav, calls the opposite view a Sadducee practice, and this account from Megillat Ta'anit is his proof.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who argued against the Sadducees.

people.name: An old man
people.about: The one Sadducee who offered an argument.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who answers an objection to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's proof from Genesis.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: In another version, the Sage who gives that answer.

terms.meaning: A Jewish group of the Second Temple period who rejected many of the Sages' traditions.
An ancient list of minor festivals, days on which fasting and eulogies were not allowed, marking happy events.
An argument from a weaker case to a stronger one: if something holds in the lesser case, all the more so in the greater.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

bava_batra-125a-5-5.note: A dying man said: my property goes to my grandmother, and after her to my heirs. He had a married daughter, who died while her husband and the grandmother were still alive. After the grandmother died, the daughter's husband claimed the property. Rav Huna said "my heirs" includes the heirs of his heirs, so the husband takes it; Rav Anan said it does not. A ruling was sent from the Land of Israel: the law follows Rav Anan, that the husband does not inherit, but for a different reason. The property was only due to the daughter, never held by her, and a husband does not inherit what is only due to his wife.
bava_batra-125a-5-5.why: Abaye and Rabba have been arguing over whether a firstborn gets a double share of debts owed to his father, and Abaye mentioned this case in passing. The Gemara stops to explain it in full.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Ruled the daughter's husband should inherit.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Ruled the husband should not inherit.

terms.meaning: Property one is only due to receive in the future, as opposed to property one already holds; a husband inherits his wife's holdings but not what was only due to her.

bava_batra-126a-9-9.note: A firstborn son sold his own share and his dead brother's share of their father's property before the estate was divided. The dead brother's orphaned sons went to eat dates from the field, and the buyers hit them. The orphans' relatives protested that the buyers had bought their property and were now beating them too. They came before Rava, who said the firstborn had done nothing: his sale was void. Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa later disagreed over whether Rava meant only the brother's share or the firstborn's extra share as well.
bava_batra-126a-9-9.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a firstborn owns his extra share before an estate is divided. It reveals that the dispute between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa was never stated outright but inferred from Rava's ruling in this case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Judge who ruled the firstborn's sale invalid.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Read Rava's ruling as voiding only the brother's share.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Read Rava's ruling as voiding the whole sale.

terms.meaning: A firstborn son receives a double share of his father's estate; the question is whether it is his before the brothers divide the estate.
A son who is not the firstborn and takes a single share.

bava_batra-132a-3-3.note: Rabbi Yehuda the baker said this happened to his sister's daughter, who was also his daughter-in-law: her husband had written her a deed giving her all his property, and then a debt against him came to light. The case came before the Sages. They said she must tear up her marriage contract and keep the deed of gift, which the creditor could collect from, so she was left bald on both sides.
bava_batra-132a-3-3.why: The Gemara is asking whether a healthy man who writes all his property to his wife truly gives it to her. A baraita and Rabbi Yehuda's case are cited as a possible proof that he does, but the Gemara rejects it, saying it may concern a dying man.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda the baker
people.about: Reports what happened to his niece, who was married to his son.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document guaranteeing a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.

terms.term: Bald from here and from there
terms.meaning: An idiom for losing on both counts: she got neither the gift nor her marriage payment.
A document recording a debt, which lets the lender collect from the borrower's property.

bava_batra-133b-5-8.note: Yosef ben Yo'ezer had a son who did not behave properly, so he consecrated a vessel full of dinars to the Temple instead of leaving it to him. The son married the daughter of King Yannai's crown weaver. When his wife gave birth, he bought her a fish and found a pearl inside. She told him not to sell it to the king's treasury, which would pay little, but to the Temple treasurers, and to let them set the price. They valued it at thirteen vessels of dinars but had only seven; he took seven and consecrated the other six. The treasurers wrote that Yosef ben Yo'ezer brought in one and his son six; others say they wrote that the son took out seven.
bava_batra-133b-5-8.why: The mishna says one who leaves his sons nothing is disliked by the Sages, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel praises it when the sons behave badly. The Gemara tries this story to see whether the Sages disagree with him, but the two versions point opposite ways, so nothing is proved.

people.name: Yosef ben Yo'ezer
people.about: Father who consecrated his money rather than leave it to his badly behaved son.

people.name: His son
people.about: Found a pearl in a fish and sold it to the Temple.

people.name: His son's wife
people.about: Daughter of King Yannai's crown weaver; advised him how to sell the pearl.

terms.meaning: Given to the Temple treasury, so it belongs to the Temple.
Officials who managed the Temple's funds.
The rule that a promise to the Temple binds at once, as fully as handing an item to a person, so a low price once named could not be taken back.

bava_batra-133b-11-12.note: A man whose children did not behave properly wrote all his property over to Yonatan ben Uzziel. Yonatan sold a third, consecrated a third to the Temple, and gave the last third back to the man's children. Shammai came to him with his staff and bag to protest. Yonatan said: if you can take back what I sold and what I consecrated, you can take back what I returned; if not, you cannot take that back either. Shammai said: ben Uzziel has rebuked me, ben Uzziel has rebuked me.
bava_batra-133b-11-12.why: The Gemara is asking whether it is right to cut children out of an inheritance; Shmuel has just warned against it. This story shows a Sage who received such a gift and gave part of it back to the children.

people.name: Yonatan ben Uzziel
people.about: Received the man's property and returned a third to his children.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Came to protest Yonatan's returning part of the gift.

terms.meaning: Given to the Temple treasury, so it belongs to the Temple.

bava_batra-134a-2-3.note: In Beit Horon, a man's father had vowed to take no benefit from him. When the man was marrying off his own son, he told a friend: the courtyard and the wedding meal are given to you as a gift, but only so that my father can come and eat with us. The friend replied: if they are mine, they are consecrated to Heaven. The man said he had not given them so the friend could consecrate them. The friend answered that the gift was only a way for father and son to eat, drink and make peace, with the sin of breaking the vow hanging on his head.
bava_batra-134a-2-3.why: The Gemara asks why Shammai first protested Yonatan ben Uzziel's handling of a gift, and answers that he had this case in mind. From it the Sages ruled that a gift the receiver could not consecrate is no gift.

people.name: The son
people.about: A man of Beit Horon whose father had vowed to take no benefit from him.

people.name: The friend
people.about: Received the courtyard and meal as a gift and declared them consecrated.

terms.meaning: A binding vow forbidding someone to get any benefit from another person, including eating his food.
Declared the property of the Temple, which forbids anyone else to use it.

bava_batra-137b-5-6.note: A woman had a palm tree on Rav Beivai bar Abaye's land, and every time she came to harvest it he got angry with her. So she transferred the tree to him for all the years of his life. He then transferred it to his young son. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said to him: because you come from a cut-short family, do you say cut-short things? Even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows such a sale only when the property was to pass to someone else afterward, not when it was to return to the giver.
bava_batra-137b-5-6.why: Rava has just ruled that a gift given on condition that it be returned is still a real gift. This case explores the limits of such a gift, which goes back to the giver after a set time.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Owner of the land where the woman's palm stood; received the tree for his lifetime.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who rejected Rav Beivai's transfer to his son.

people.name: A certain woman
people.about: Owner of the palm tree, who gave it to Rav Beivai for his lifetime.

terms.meaning: A wordplay: Rav Beivai's family traced its line to Eli, whose descendants were cursed with early death, so Rav Huna calls his reasoning cut short too.

bava_batra-142b-7-7.note: A man told his wife, before she had conceived: my property goes to the sons I will have with you. His older son from an earlier marriage came and asked: and what will become of me? The father told him: go and acquire like one of those sons. The Gemara notes that the unborn sons certainly acquired nothing, since they did not yet exist.
bava_batra-142b-7-7.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a fetus cannot acquire property given to it. This case of a gift to sons not yet conceived follows, and the Sages then argue over whether the older son got anything extra.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: Promised his property to the sons he would have with his wife.

people.name: His older son
people.about: Son from an earlier marriage who asked what he would receive.

bava_batra-144a-1-1.note: Rav Safra's father left him money, and Rav Safra took it and went into business with it. His brothers took him to court before Rava, claiming a share of the profits. Rava told them: Rav Safra is a great man; he would not leave his studies to toil for others.
bava_batra-144a-1-1.why: The mishna rules that heirs who said from the start that they are trading with their own share keep the profit. Rava's ruling shows that a man like Rav Safra is treated as if he had said so, even without saying it.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Invested the money his father left and was sued by his brothers.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Judge who ruled the profits were Rav Safra's.

bava_batra-146a-5-6.note: Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, told of a man who sent his father-in-law's house a hundred wagons of wine and oil, a hundred of silver vessels, a hundred of gold vessels and a hundred of fine wool garments. He rode over in his joy and stood at the entrance; they brought out a cup of a hot drink, he drank it, and he died. Rabbi Aha Sar HaBira raised the case before the Sages in Usha, and they said that gifts meant to be used up are not returned, and those not meant to be used up are returned.
bava_batra-146a-5-6.why: The mishna says a betrothed man who ate a groom's feast at his father-in-law's cannot reclaim his gifts, and the Gemara asks whether drinking counts. It reads this case as proof that drinking does.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: A betrothed man who sent great gifts and died at his father-in-law's door.

people.name: Rabbi Aha Sar HaBira
people.about: Brought the case before the Sages in Usha.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which binds the couple before the wedding when they begin to live together.
Gifts a betrothed man sends to his bride's family; the question is when they must be returned if the marriage does not happen.
A town in the Galilee where the Sages met as a court.

bava_batra-146a-12-12.note: Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, told of a man who heard that his betrothed had lost her sense of smell. He followed her into a ruin, carrying a date, to test her. He said: I smell the scent of radish in the Galilee. She said: who will give us of the dates of Jericho to eat, showing she had smelled his date. The ruin fell on her and she died. The Sages said that since he went in after her only to test her, he does not inherit from her.
bava_batra-146a-12-12.why: It follows another incident Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name, in the Gemara's discussion of what a betrothed man and his bride's family owe each other when a betrothal never becomes a marriage.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: A betrothed man who tested his bride's sense of smell.

people.name: His wife
people.about: His betrothed, who was killed when the ruin collapsed.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage; a betrothed couple are legally bound but have not yet begun married life, and the man does not inherit from her.

bava_batra-149a-2-4.note: Issur, a convert, had twelve thousand dinars on deposit with Rava. His son, Rav Mari, had been conceived before Issur converted and born after, and was away at a study hall when his father lay dying. Rava reasoned aloud that Rav Mari had no way to get the money: he could not inherit it, a deathbed gift counts like inheritance, the coins were not in his hands to pull, coins cannot be acquired by symbolic exchange, Issur owned no land to attach them to, and a transfer in the presence of all three parties needed Rava himself, who said he would not come if sent for. The text here stops before telling how it turned out.
bava_batra-149a-2-4.why: The Gemara asks whether a dying man's admission that he owes someone money works like a deathbed gift, and opens this case with 'come and hear' as the proof.

people.name: Issur the convert
people.about: A convert who had deposited twelve thousand dinars with Rava and was on his deathbed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage holding Issur's money, who reasons that Rav Mari cannot acquire it.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Issur's son, conceived before his father converted and born after; away at a study hall.

terms.meaning: A formal way of transferring ownership in which the buyer hands over an object, often a cloth, to seal the deal. The Sages held that coins cannot be transferred this way.

terms.term: in the presence of all three
terms.meaning: A way of transferring money held by a third party: the owner tells the holder, in front of the recipient, to hold it for the recipient instead. It needs all three people there.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: A gift made by someone who expects to die soon. The Sages let it take effect by words alone, without the usual formal acts of acquisition, and treated it like inheritance.

bava_batra-151a-4-4.note: The mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviyya wrote her property over to her son, saying she did it because she wanted to marry Rav Zevid. She married him, and he divorced her. She then came before Rav Beivai bar Abaye to get her property back. Rav Beivai ruled against her: she gave the property because she wanted to marry, and she did marry, so the gift stands.
bava_batra-151a-4-4.why: This opens a string of cases, listed by a memory aid just before it, about gifts of property and when they can be taken back. Right after it Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, attacks Rav Beivai's ruling, saying she had stated her reason and the marriage ended.

people.name: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya
people.about: The son to whom his mother wrote over her property.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The man she wanted to marry; he married her and then divorced her.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: The judge she came to for her property; he ruled the gift valid.

terms.meaning: A written document transferring ownership. Here a woman about to marry uses one to put her property in her son's name so that her new husband does not get it.

bava_batra-151a-6-7.note: The mother of Rami bar Hama wrote her property over to him one evening, then wrote it over to his brother, Rav Ukva bar Hama, the next morning. Rami went to Rav Sheshet, who gave him the property; Rav Ukva went to Rav Nahman, who gave it to him. Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman: she has died, so how could she have retracted? Rav Nahman answered with Shmuel's teaching that whenever a dying person could have retracted the gift had he recovered, he can retract it even without recovering.
bava_batra-151a-6-7.why: This is one of a string of cases about deathbed gifts. It turns on whether a dying woman who gave away everything can change her mind and give it to someone else, which Rav Sheshet presses further right after.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The son who received his mother's property in the evening; Rav Sheshet ruled for him.

people.name: Rav Ukva bar Hama
people.about: His brother, who received the same property the next morning; Rav Nahman ruled for him.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The judge who ruled for Rami and then questioned Rav Nahman's ruling.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who ruled for Rav Ukva, citing Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Nahman quotes.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: A gift made by someone who expects to die soon. If such a person gives away all his property and then recovers, he can take the gift back.
To take back a gift already given.

bava_batra-151a-9-9.note: The mother of Rav Amram the Pious had a bundle of promissory notes. As she was dying she said: Let them be for Amram, my son. His brothers went to Rav Nahman and objected that Amram had never pulled the bundle, the formal act that transfers ownership. Rav Nahman told them that the words of a dying person count as if written and handed over.
bava_batra-151a-9-9.why: One of a string of deathbed-gift cases ruled by Rav Nahman. This one shows that a dying person's spoken words alone transfer even documents, with no formal act of acquisition.

people.name: Rav Amram the Pious
people.about: The son to whom his dying mother left her bundle of promissory notes.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who upheld the gift against the brothers' objection.

terms.meaning: Written records of loans that entitle the holder to collect the debt.
A formal way of taking ownership of movable things: the new owner physically draws the item toward himself.

bava_batra-151a-10-10.note: The sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana wrote her property over to Rav Tovi one morning. That evening another brother, Rav Ahadvoi bar Rav Mattana, came to her crying and said people would now say that one brother is a Torah scholar and the other is not. So she wrote the property over to him. Rav Tovi came before Rav Nahman, who quoted Shmuel: whenever a dying person could have retracted the gift had he recovered, he can retract it, and so the property went to Rav Ahadvoi.
bava_batra-151a-10-10.why: Another case in the string of deathbed gifts, applying the rule Rav Nahman has just stated: a dying person who gave away everything may give it again to someone else.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: The brother who received his sister's property in the morning and lost it.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: Another brother, who cried to his sister and got the property that evening.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge, who ruled for Rav Ahadvoi by quoting Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Nahman quotes.

terms.meaning: Someone learned in Jewish law and teaching. Rav Ahadvoi feared people would think his sister favored Rav Tovi for being one.

bava_batra-151a-11-11.note: The sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef owned part of an orchard. Each time she fell sick she gave it to him, and each time she recovered she took it back. Once, sick again, she sent for him; he refused to come until she told him to acquire it any way he liked, so he left part of it to her and took the rest with a formal act. When she recovered she took it back and went to Rav Nahman. Rav Dimi would not come to court, and Rav Nahman threatened to strike him with a thorn that does not draw blood. Rav Nahman asked the witnesses what had happened; they said she had cried, 'Woe, that woman is dying!' He ruled that she had given it in expectation of death, so she could retract.
bava_batra-151a-11-11.why: Rav Dimi relied on the rule that a dying person who keeps back part of his property cannot take the gift back. The story shows Rav Nahman making an exception when the gift was clearly made only because death was expected.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: The brother who received his sister's orchard and tried to make the gift stick.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who summoned Rav Dimi, threatened him, and ruled for the sister.

terms.term: thorn that does not draw blood
terms.meaning: Rav Nahman's threat; the translation explains it as excommunication, a ban that cuts a person off from the community.
Kept back part of the property for the giver. A dying person who gives away only part of his property normally cannot take it back if he recovers.

terms.term: one who issues directives due to death
terms.meaning: A person who gives away property only because he expects to die. Rav Nahman rules that such a gift can be taken back.

bava_batra-151b-7-7.note: The mother of the sons of Rokhel was sick and said: My brooch, worth twelve hundred dinars, shall be given to my daughter. She died, and the Sages upheld her words. Rav Mesharshiyya raised this incident against Rava, and Rava answered that she had spoken in expectation of her death.
bava_batra-151b-7-7.why: Rava has just said, in Rav Nahman's name, that a deathbed gift of only part of one's property needs a formal act of acquisition. This incident, a part-gift upheld without one, is raised as an objection to him.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as an objection to Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who answers the objection.

people.name: the mother of the sons of Rokhel
people.about: A sick woman who left her valuable brooch to her daughter.

terms.term: one who issues directives due to death
terms.meaning: A person who gives away property only because he expects to die. Rava says such a gift is a special case.

bava_batra-153a-7-9.note: A man whose deed said his gift was given in life and in death came before Rav Nahman in Neharde'a. Rav Nahman sent him to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in Shum Tamya, saying that Neharde'a was Shmuel's town, so how could he rule there like Rav? Later a woman with a deed reading 'during life and in death' came before Rava, who ruled by his own teaching that she could not retract. She kept troubling him. Rava told his scribe, Rav Pappa son of Rav Hanan, to write her a ruling with a phrase meant to show it was a ruse. She saw through it and said: May his ship sink, you are deceiving me. Rava had his clothes dunked in water to fulfill the curse, but his ship sank anyway.
bava_batra-153a-7-9.why: The Gemara has been debating how to read a deed that says a gift is given 'in life and in death', and whether it can be retracted. These two incidents show Rav Nahman and Rava acting on that dispute.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a who would not rule against Shmuel's view in Shmuel's own town.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage in Shum Tamya to whom Rav Nahman sent the man.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge whose ruling the woman would not accept, and whom she cursed.

people.name: Rav Pappa, son of Rav Hanan
people.about: Rava's scribe, told to write the woman's ruling.

terms.meaning: Neharde'a, where Shmuel taught. Judges there followed his rulings over those of Rav, who held a different view on this kind of deed.

terms.term: hire replacements at their expense, or deceive them
terms.meaning: A phrase from a teaching about workers who quit; Rava had it written into the ruling to signal that the ruling was only a trick to send the woman away.

bava_batra-154a-10-10.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether the body could be examined. He told them they were not permitted to disgrace him, and that the signs of puberty change after death anyway. Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish then argue over what the incident shows.
bava_batra-154a-10-10.why: Rabbi Yohanan says proof in such disputes must come from witnesses, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says ratifying the deed is enough. Rabbi Yohanan raises the Bnei Brak incident against him, and they debate who held the property and who was bringing the challenge.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the family asked; he forbade examining the body.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who raises the incident as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: The Sage who answers Rabbi Yohanan's objection.

terms.meaning: Someone not yet legally adult. A minor's sale of land he inherited is not valid, so the relatives claimed the seller was still one.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law. This incident is quoted from one.
Confirming in court that the signatures on a document are genuine, which makes the document valid evidence.

bava_batra-155a-3-3.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had been a minor when he died, and asked Rabbi Akiva whether the body could be examined. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and that signs of puberty change after death. Rabbi Zeira uses the incident in a discussion of the age at which a young heir may sell, which leads on to Rabbi Hiyya's practice: when a man without signs of puberty came before him, he would tell them to fatten him if he was thin, or thin him if he was fat.
bava_batra-155a-3-3.why: The Gemara is asking whether an heir can sell his father's land from age eighteen or only from twenty. Rabbi Zeira argues that examining the body would only make sense under the age-eighteen view, and the Gemara answers him.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the family asked; he forbade examining the body.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who raises the incident as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who taught how long a man without signs of puberty counts as a minor, and advised changing his weight.

terms.meaning: Physical signs, such as two pubic hairs, that Jewish law uses to decide when a young person becomes a legal adult.
A man who never develops signs of puberty but shows other signs of this condition; at twenty he is treated as an adult.
The ceremony that frees a childless widow from having to marry her late husband's brother. The underdeveloped man takes no part in it.

bava_batra-155b-7-8.note: A young man under twenty sold his father's property and the case came before Rava. His relatives told him to eat dates and throw the pits into Rava's house; he did, and Rava ruled the sale invalid. While the ruling was being written, the buyers told him to ask Rava why the scroll of Esther costs a dinar and the Master's short document also costs a dinar. He asked, and Rava ruled the sale valid. When the relatives said the buyers had coached him, Rava replied that since he understands when things are explained to him, he knows what he is doing, and the date pits were just excessive impudence.
bava_batra-155b-7-8.why: Rava taught that a girl of fourteen who understands business can sell. The Gemara says this ruling of his was not stated outright but inferred from this case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who first voided the young man's sale, then upheld it.

people.name: Giddel bar Menashya
people.about: The man whose question to Rava gave the ruling this young man was relying on.

terms.meaning: The long handwritten scroll of the Book of Esther, read on Purim. The young man's question compares its price to the scribe's fee for Rava's short ruling.
A silver coin; here the price of a scroll of Esther and the fee for writing the court document.

bava_batra-156b-1-2.note: Rabbi Eliezer told the Rabbis about a man from Meron who was in Jerusalem and had a great deal of movable property he wanted to give away. He was told there was no way to do it except by attaching the goods to a transfer of land. So he bought a plot of rocky land near Jerusalem and said: The north part goes to so-and-so, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, and the south part to so-and-so, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He died, and the Sages upheld his words. The Rabbis answered that there was no proof here, since the man from Meron had been healthy.
bava_batra-156b-1-2.why: Rabbi Elazar holds that even a dying man's gifts need the usual formal acts of transfer. The Rabbis had cited the Rokhel brooch case against him; here the Gemara quotes his own case in reply, and the Rabbis reject it.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who tells the Rabbis this incident.

people.name: the man of Meron
people.about: A man in Jerusalem who wanted to give away his many movable goods.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be carried or led, like sheep and barrels, as opposed to land.
A legal device: movable goods can be transferred along with a piece of land, so the transfer of the land carries them.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna; this exchange is quoted from one.

bava_batra-159b-9-10.note: A man told another: I am selling you the property of bar Sisin. One field was known as the field of the house of bar Sisin, and the seller said it was not really bar Sisin's property, only called that. The case came before Rav Nahman, who gave the field to the buyer. Rava challenged him: Is this the law? The one who wants to take something from another must bring the proof.
bava_batra-159b-9-10.why: The Gemara sets this case beside another in which Rav Nahman and Rava seem to take the opposite sides, and asks how each Sage can be consistent with himself.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who gave the disputed field to the buyer.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who objected that the buyer should have had to bring proof.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: A basic rule of Jewish civil law: whoever wants to take property from the person holding it must prove his claim.

bava_batra-159b-11-12.note: A man asked another what he was doing in his house. The other answered that he had bought it from him and had lived in it long enough to establish ownership. The owner said he had been away among distant settlements. The case came before Rav Nahman, who told the occupant to go and prove he had lived there. Rava objected: Is this the law? The one who wants to take something from another must bring the proof.
bava_batra-159b-11-12.why: The Gemara sets this case against the bar Sisin case just before it, where Rav Nahman and Rava each took the opposite side, and goes on to explain why their rulings do not contradict each other.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who told the occupant to prove his years of residence.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who objected that the claimant should bear the burden of proof.

terms.meaning: A rule that someone who has openly used a property for three years without protest is presumed to own it, even without a deed.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: A basic rule: whoever wants to take property from the person holding it must prove his claim.

bava_batra-164b-12-12.note: A tied document came before Rabbi, and he said there was no date on it. His son, Rabbi Shimon, suggested the date might be hidden between the folds. Rabbi opened it and found the date there, then looked at his son with displeasure. His son said: I did not write it, Rabbi Yehuda Hayyata wrote it. Rabbi told him: Turn away from this malicious speech.
bava_batra-164b-12-12.why: The discussion has been about tied documents, folded and signed on the back, and how they are written. This incident about one leads straight into a second like it and into a teaching on malicious speech.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he found the hidden date and rebuked his son.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi's son, who guessed where the date was and named the writer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Hayyata
people.about: The man Rabbi Shimon says wrote the document.

terms.meaning: A document folded over and tied, with witnesses signing on the back between the folds, so that parts of the text, such as the date, are hidden inside.
Saying things about another person that can harm him, even when true. Jewish teaching counts it as a serious sin.

bava_batra-164b-13-13.note: Another time Rabbi Shimon was sitting before his father, Rabbi, reading a section of Psalms. Rabbi said: How straight this writing is! Rabbi Shimon said: I did not write it, Yehuda Hayyata wrote it. Rabbi told him: Turn away from this malicious speech.
bava_batra-164b-13-13.why: It follows a similar exchange about a tied document. The Gemara then asks why mere praise counts as malicious speech, and answers that praise of a person can lead others to speak against him.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi's son, reading from Psalms.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who praised the writing and rebuked his son.

people.name: Yehuda Hayyata
people.about: The man Rabbi Shimon says wrote the book.

terms.meaning: Saying things about another person that can harm him. The Gemara goes on to say that even praise can lead to it.

bava_batra-166a-6-6.note: Once in Jerusalem the price of a pair of birds for offerings rose to golden dinars. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel swore by the Temple that he would not go to sleep that night until the price was down to silver dinars. He went into the court and taught that a woman with five definite births or five definite discharges brings one offering and may eat from offerings, and the rest are not required of her. That same day the price fell to a quarter of a silver dinar.
bava_batra-166a-6-6.why: The Gemara is proving that two plural forms of 'dinar' mean different coins, gold and silver. This incident, from a mishna on women's offerings, shows the two words used for very different prices.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who swore to bring the price down and changed the ruling in court.

terms.meaning: Pairs of birds, the offering a woman brought after childbirth or after an irregular discharge of blood.
A woman who has had an irregular discharge of blood from the uterus; she must bring an offering when she becomes pure.
Two plural forms of dinar. The Gemara says the first refers to gold dinars and the second to silver ones, which are worth far less.

bava_batra-167a-2-2.note: A tax collector came to Abaye and asked to see his signature, so that when rabbis showed him notes signed by Abaye he could let them pass without paying the tax. Abaye signed at the top of the parchment, but the tax collector kept pulling it so the signature would land at the bottom. Abaye said to him: The Sages already anticipated you.
bava_batra-167a-2-2.why: Abaye has just taught that one should never show one's signature at the bottom of a sheet, since someone could write a debt above it. This incident shows him following his own rule.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage whose signature the tax collector wanted; he signed at the top.

terms.meaning: Treated animal skin used as writing material for documents.

bava_batra-167a-4-4.note: A bill of sale said the buyer was getting one third of an orchard. The buyer erased the top and bottom of one letter so that it read 'one third, and the orchard', claiming the whole orchard. When it came before Abaye, he asked why there was so much space around that letter. He had the buyer bound, and the buyer admitted it.
bava_batra-167a-4-4.why: The Gemara is collecting Abaye's warnings and cases about forged documents; just before, he taught where to place numbers so they cannot be altered. This is one of his forgery cases.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The judge who spotted the forgery from the spacing of the letters.

terms.meaning: A written document recording what was sold.
Two Hebrew letters. Turning the wide beit, meaning 'of', into the narrow vav, meaning 'and', changed 'a third of the orchard' into 'a third, and the orchard'.

bava_batra-167a-5-5.note: A bill of sale gave the buyer the portions of Reuven and Shimon, brothers. They had a third brother named Ahai, a name spelled like the word for 'brothers'. The buyer added one letter so that it read 'Reuven and Shimon and Ahai', claiming the third brother's share too. When it came before Abaye, he asked why the letters were so crowded around that added letter. He had the buyer bound, and the buyer admitted it.
bava_batra-167a-5-5.why: It is the second in a run of forgery cases brought before Abaye, after his teaching on how to write documents so they cannot be altered.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The judge who spotted the forgery from the crowded letters.

people.name: Reuven
people.about: One of the brothers whose portion was sold.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: One of the brothers whose portion was sold.

people.name: Ahai
people.about: Their brother, whose share the buyer tried to add by forgery.

terms.meaning: A written document recording what was sold.
A narrow Hebrew letter meaning 'and'. Squeezing one in turned 'brothers' into 'and Ahai'.

bava_batra-167a-6-6.note: A document carried the signatures of two witnesses, Rava and Rav Aha bar Adda. Its holder brought it before Rava, who said: this is my signature, but I never signed anything together with Rav Aha bar Adda. Rava bound the man and he admitted the forgery. Rava then asked how he had copied Rav Aha bar Adda's signature, since that Sage's hands shake. The man said he had rested his hands on the rope of a narrow footbridge; some say he stood on a wobbly water skin as he wrote.
bava_batra-167a-6-6.why: The Gemara has been discussing forged documents: Abaye's warning about where numbers fall on a line, and two altered bills of sale that Abaye exposed. This third case is caught by one of the supposed signers himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose real signature appears on the forged document; he exposes the forger.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Adda
people.about: A Sage whose hands shake, so his signature is distinctive; his signature was forged.

terms.meaning: Subjected to physical coercion, used here by the judge to force the holder of a suspect document to confess.

bava_batra-168a-1-1.note: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba had signed as a witness on a receipt showing that a woman had been paid her marriage contract. A woman whose name was on the receipt told him: it was not I. He answered her: but it was you. Abaye said that although a Torah scholar does not usually look closely at women to identify them, once he does say he is sure, his identification holds.
bava_batra-168a-1-1.why: Just before, the Gemara told a version in which Rav Yirmeya doubted the woman's identity and Abaye let him retract his signature. This version has him identifying her firmly, and Abaye explains why that changes things.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: A Sage who signed as a witness on the woman's receipt.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who comments on how far a scholar's identification of a woman can be trusted.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife at marriage, promising her a sum of money if he divorces her or dies.
A signed document showing a woman has already collected her marriage contract, so she cannot collect it again.

bava_batra-168b-5-8.note: A band of Arabs came to Pumbedita and seized people's land. Landowners asked Abaye to write a second deed for each property, so that if one were taken they would still hold the other. Abaye said he could not, since Rav Safra rules that two deeds are not written for one field. They kept badgering him, so he told his scribe to write the deeds over erased writing, with the witnesses signing on unerased paper, which makes a document invalid. Rav Aha bar Minyumi objected that if the erased writing were still legible the deed would be valid. Abaye answered that he had meant the scribe to write and erase only letters of the alphabet, not a real document.
bava_batra-168b-5-8.why: The Gemara has just cited a baraita that a document erased or smudged is valid if its writing can still be made out. Rav Aha bar Minyumi applies that very ruling to Abaye's trick.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage the landowners ask for duplicate deeds.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage whose ruling against writing two deeds for one field Abaye cites.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Minyumi
people.about: A Sage who challenges Abaye's instructions to the scribe.

terms.meaning: A document proving ownership of land.

When land is taken from a buyer by the seller's creditor or a rightful owner, the buyer can collect his loss from the seller's other sold land by showing his deed. Two deeds could let him collect twice.

bava_batra-169b-9-10.note: A woman gave a man money to buy land for her as her agent. He bought the land without a guarantee. She came before Rav Nahman, who told the agent that she could say: I sent you to help me, not to harm me, so the purchase made on her behalf was void. Rav Nahman told the agent to buy the land from the seller himself without a guarantee, and then sell it to her with one.
bava_batra-169b-9-10.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a bill of sale that leaves out the guarantee still carries one. This case of an agent who bought without a guarantee is set beside that debate.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage the woman brings her complaint to.

terms.meaning: A seller's promise to repay the buyer if the land is later taken away by the seller's creditor or by someone who proves it belongs to him.
Someone appointed to act for another; what he does on the appointer's behalf counts as if the appointer did it.

bava_batra-170a-16-17.note: Rabbi Abba owed money to Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, and the case came before Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha. Rabbi Abba said he had repaid the debt in front of two named people. The judge said those two must come and testify. Rabbi Abba protested that a borrower need not repay in front of witnesses. The judge answered that he was following Rabbi Abba's own teaching, in Rav's name: whoever says he repaid in front of named people must bring them. Rabbi Abba cited a ruling that follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the judge replied that he only meant Rabbi Abba should bring them if he could.
bava_batra-170a-16-17.why: The Gemara has just suggested that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree about whether a litigant must back up a claim he did not need to make. This case is its example of that kind of verifying.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: The lender, owed money by Rabbi Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The borrower, who says he already repaid.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: The judge who hears the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.

bava_batra-171b-5-6.note: Rabbi Abba owed money to Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, and they came before the judge Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. Rabbi Abba said he would pay once he got his promissory note back; Rav Yitzhak said he had lost it and offered to write a receipt instead. Rabbi Abba cited Rav and Shmuel, who rule that no receipt is written. The judge said he honored Rav and Shmuel so much he would put their dust on his eyes, but Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish both rule that a receipt is written.
bava_batra-171b-5-6.why: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said a receipt is never written when a whole debt is repaid; the Gemara disagrees and brings this case to prove that it is.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: The lender, who had lost the promissory note.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The borrower, who would not pay without getting the note back.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
people.about: The Sage who served as judge in the case.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: The two great early Sages of Babylonia, often cited as a pair.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
people.about: The two great Sages of the Land of Israel in their generation, study partners.

terms.meaning: A written loan document. Normally it is handed back or torn up when the debt is paid, so it cannot be used to collect a second time.
A signed document saying the debt was paid, written for the borrower when the note itself cannot be returned.

bava_batra-174a-10-11.note: A judge let a creditor take over a debtor's property to collect his debt before the creditor had made any claim against the debtor himself. Rav Hanin, son of Rav Yeiva, overruled the judge and expelled the creditor. Rava said: who is wise enough to rule this way, if not Rav Hanin? Rava explained that a person's property acts as his guarantor, and a creditor may not collect from a guarantor before first claiming from the debtor.
bava_batra-174a-10-11.why: The Gemara has been discussing guarantors and when a creditor may turn to them. Rava stretches the rule that a guarantor is not approached first to cover the debtor's own property.

people.name: Rav Hanin, son of Rav Yeiva
people.about: A Sage who overrules the judge and removes the creditor from the property.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who praises Rav Hanin's ruling and explains it.

terms.meaning: A person who promises to pay a loan if the borrower does not.
The early collection of the Sages' rulings that the Gemara discusses.

bava_batra-174a-12-14.note: A man had guaranteed a loan. The borrower died, leaving orphans who were minors, and the guarantor repaid the creditor before telling them. He then wanted the orphans to repay him. Rav Pappa said repaying a creditor is a mitzva, and minor orphans are not obligated in mitzvot. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said perhaps the father had handed the creditor bundles of money before he died. The Gemara asks where the two reasons differ, and answers: when the father admitted before dying that he had not paid, or when he died while excommunicated over the debt.
bava_batra-174a-12-14.why: The case before it involved a creditor who collected before claiming from the debtor. Here a guarantor paid first, and the Gemara goes on to a ruling sent from the Land of Israel that follows Rav Huna in the excommunication case.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who exempts minor orphans because they are not obligated in mitzvot.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who exempts them because their father may already have paid.

terms.meaning: A commandment; a religious duty.
Money the dead man may have handed the creditor before his death, which his young children would not know about.
Placed under a ban by the court; here, for refusing to cooperate in repaying a debt.

bava_batra-174b-8-10.note: Moshe bar Atzari had guaranteed the marriage contract of his daughter-in-law. His son, Rav Huna, was a young Torah scholar who was short of money. Abaye asked: is there no one to advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife, so she can collect her marriage contract from his father, and then remarry her? Rava objected that the mishna requires such a husband to vow to take no benefit from her. Abaye replied that not everyone who divorces does so in court. In the end it came out that Rav Huna was a priest, who may not marry a divorcee. Abaye said: as people say, poverty follows the poor.
bava_batra-174b-8-10.why: The mishna quotes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a husband whose wife's marriage contract has a guarantor must vow off her when he divorces her, to block exactly this ploy. Afterward the Gemara asks how Abaye could suggest it when he condemned such advice elsewhere.

people.name: Moshe bar Atzari
people.about: Guarantor of his daughter-in-law's marriage contract; Rav Huna's father.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Moshe bar Atzari's son, a young Torah scholar short of money, who turns out to be a priest.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who proposes the divorce-and-remarry plan.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects to Abaye's plan.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife at marriage, promising her a sum of money if he divorces her or dies.
Someone who promises to pay if the person primarily responsible does not.
The early collection of the Sages' rulings that the Gemara discusses.
